name: Airy Labs
tagline: Educational games for kids, minus the focus to make any of them great
proximateCause: ran out of cash
rootCause: spread itself across too many game titles at once instead of focusing on one, burning cash on breadth instead of depth
timingNote: not a timing problem — the mobile app boom was real and happening; the failure was self-inflicted execution sprawl, not the market being unready

name: Bebo
tagline: The UK's biggest social network, bought once to save it and once just to strip it for esports parts
description: Social networking site popular in UK
proximateCause: users and cultural relevance had already moved to Facebook years before Twitch's 2019 acquisition
rootCause: AOL's 2008 acquisition mismanaged the platform and starved it of investment while Facebook's network effects compounded internationally; by the time it was sold to Twitch for esports in 2019, it was a spare-parts deal for the brand, not a comeback
timingNote: timing mattered — Bebo peaked right before Facebook opened to the public and scaled internationally; AOL's neglect meant it had no answer when that wave hit, and every later revival attempt landed in a market Facebook already owned

name: Auctionata
tagline: Brought the auction house online, then couldn't make the economics or the trust hold up
description: Online auction house for art and luxury
proximateCause: insolvency driven by high operating costs
rootCause: the white-glove, high-touch auction model (in-house experts, live-streamed auctions, authentication) carried costs that didn't scale, and a public valuation/authentication scandal undermined the trust the luxury-auction business model depended on
timingNote: not a timing problem — online luxury auctions were a real, growing category; the failure was operational (cost structure) and reputational (scandal), not the market being unready

name: Boxed
tagline: Costco without the membership fee, but also without Amazon's shipping scale
proximateCause: filed for bankruptcy under the weight of shipping and fulfillment costs
rootCause: the bulk-buying convenience model required expensive last-mile shipping of heavy, low-margin bulk goods — a cost structure Amazon could absorb at its scale but Boxed couldn't match without it
timingNote: not primarily a timing issue — bulk e-commerce demand existed throughout; the failure was a structural cost disadvantage against a competitor with vastly greater shipping scale, not a market that closed

name: Scanadu
tagline: Built a real-life tricorder, then the FDA said the science project had to end
proximateCause: the FDA required Scanadu to deactivate its Scout devices once its investigational study concluded
rootCause: Scanadu sold and shipped the Scout as a consumer device funded via crowdfunding while it was still legally an investigational device under an IRB-approved study; when the study reached its endpoint, FDA rules forced it to shut down devices customers had already paid for and were using, with no cleared consumer product ready to replace it
timingNote: a timing mismatch, but not a market one — Scanadu got ahead of its own regulatory pathway, shipping to consumers before it had a clear route to full FDA clearance, so the regulatory clock ran out before the business model matured

name: Basis
tagline: A promising health smartwatch, discontinued after it started burning wrists
proximateCause: Intel issued a full recall and shut down the Basis Peak after reports of overheating and skin burns
rootCause: the watch's continuous LED heart-rate sensor could overheat under certain conditions and cause burns; once Intel couldn't engineer a fix, it was cheaper and safer to recall and discontinue the whole product line than keep competing against Fitbit and Apple Watch with an unresolved safety flaw
timingNote: not a timing problem — wearable fitness tracking was a booming category at the time; the failure was a hardware safety defect that had nothing to do with market readiness

name: Simple
tagline: One of the first neobanks, killed by its parent company's own acquisition, not by the market
proximateCause: shut down after its acquirer BBVA was itself acquired and exited the business
rootCause: Simple ceded strategic control by selling to BBVA early, and once BBVA was acquired by PNC, Simple had no independent path forward while faster-growing independents like Chime and Ally captured the neobank market on their own terms
timingNote: timing worked against it in a specific way — it was early to neobanking but lost strategic independence just as the category was taking off, so it couldn't capture the growth its early-mover position should have earned

name: Pawngo
tagline: Took pawnshops online, but the customers who use pawnshops wanted them in person
proximateCause: couldn't generate enough loan volume to sustain the business
rootCause: online pawn lending removed the in-person trust and immediacy that make pawnshops useful to their core customers, so it competed against an entrenched offline habit without offering a compelling enough advantage to shift behavior
timingNote: not a timing issue — the niche itself was structurally small and tied to in-person behavior; waiting longer wouldn't have grown the addressable market

name: Anki
tagline: Built genuinely impressive robots, at a price no toy aisle could sustain
proximateCause: high per-unit hardware costs made the product too expensive to compete at consumer toy price points
rootCause: building AI-driven robotics into a toy meant hardware costs that couldn't come down to compete with cheaper, established players like Lego and Sphero, so its price stayed too high for the mass-market toy audience it needed
timingNote: not a timing failure — the cost structure of the hardware was the constraint at any point in time, not a market that wasn't ready yet

name: Flowtab
tagline: Wanted to change how you order a drink; bars just kept using their POS systems
proximateCause: low adoption among bars and customers
rootCause: asked bars to change ordering behavior and adopt a new app layer on top of existing point-of-sale systems, and neither bars nor customers saw enough incremental convenience to justify switching from the POS systems already in place
timingNote: not a timing problem — the friction was behavioral and structural (integrating with existing POS systems), not a market condition that would resolve itself with more time

name: Burbn
tagline: The multi-feature check-in app that got reduced to its one good idea, and that idea became Instagram
proximateCause: the app was cluttered and low-engagement as a check-in/gaming/photo product
rootCause: Burbn combined check-ins, plans-making, and photo-sharing into one app; when usage data showed photo-sharing was the only feature people actually used, the founders killed everything else and rebuilt around it as Instagram
timingNote: not a timing failure — the founders caught the smartphone-photo wave at exactly the right moment; the product just had the wrong shape until it was stripped down

name: Color Labs
tagline: Raised $41M and a wave of hype before anyone understood what the app actually did
proximateCause: users found the product confusing and didn't adopt it
rootCause: Color's location-based, contactless photo-sharing concept asked users to learn a genuinely new social model right as Instagram was winning with a simpler one (follow people, see their photos), so the pre-launch hype never converted into real usage
timingNote: timing worked against it — it launched right as Instagram was defining and winning the category with a simpler model, leaving no room for a more confusing alternative to find its footing

name: Factual
tagline: A location-data platform that made more sense merged with its biggest rival than standing alone
proximateCause: merged into Foursquare rather than continuing as an independent competitor
rootCause: location data became a scale game dominated by Google Maps' first-party data advantage; two mid-sized independent players (Factual and Foursquare) combining was a defensive move to pool data and compete, which is itself evidence neither could win alone
timingNote: not a pure timing issue — the location-data category consolidated broadly around this time as smaller players found they couldn't match Google's scale independently

name: Digg
tagline: A redesign so unpopular it accidentally launched its own killer
proximateCause: a 2010 redesign gutted the features and community mechanics users relied on
rootCause: Digg's 'version 4' relaunch removed the community-driven bury button and shifted the algorithm to favor publishers over user submissions, alienating the power users who had built the site's front page; those users mass-migrated to Reddit within weeks, and the site never recovered before being sold off cheaply
timingNote: not a market-timing problem — social news aggregation was thriving; the failure was a self-inflicted product decision that handed an entire engaged community to a direct competitor almost overnight

name: Formspring
tagline: The anonymous Q&A app that couldn't outrun the bullying it enabled
proximateCause: cyberbullying on the platform, including cases linked to teen suicides, drove users and advertisers away
rootCause: Formspring's core anonymity feature was also its core liability; once bullying became severe enough to trigger public backlash, the company had to curb the very anonymity that made the product distinctive, which killed engagement without solving the underlying trust problem
timingNote: not a timing issue — anonymous Q&A apps had a real audience; the failure was that the product's defining feature and its worst harm were the same mechanism

name: RethinkDB
tagline: Open-source engineers loved it; almost nobody paid for it
proximateCause: the company couldn't convert its open-source user base into enough paying enterprise customers
rootCause: RethinkDB built a technically well-regarded NoSQL database, but the industry's shift toward cloud-managed database services meant customers increasingly wanted a hosted product rather than software to run themselves; RethinkDB never built that hosted business fast enough to fund the underlying open-source engineering
timingNote: a timing problem, but not the commonly assumed one — it wasn't beaten by MongoDB on features, it was overtaken by the broader industry shift to cloud-managed databases before it built a monetization model around that shift

name: Secret
tagline: Built for candor, shut down by its own worst users
proximateCause: the app's founder shut it down after concluding it was mostly being used for defamatory and mean-spirited posts
rootCause: Secret's anonymity model removed accountability at the exact layer (naming real people) where accountability mattered most, so the app's most viral use case became targeted harassment rather than the candid, low-stakes sharing it was designed for
timingNote: not a timing problem — anonymous sharing apps had real usage in this window; the failure was a direct, foreseeable consequence of the product's core design choice, not a market that wasn't ready

name: Maker Media
tagline: Make: magazine and Maker Faire ran out of sponsors before they ran out of makers
proximateCause: the company couldn't cover print and event costs and ceased operations abruptly, laying off all 22 employees
rootCause: Maker Media depended on corporate sponsorship and investor funding to subsidize money-losing print publishing and live events; when sponsorship and investor interest dried up, there was no cash cushion left to keep the business running
timingNote: not a timing problem for the underlying maker movement, which stayed active — the failure was a monetization model (print plus events) that never became self-sustaining; the founder relaunched a smaller version under new ownership almost immediately after

name: Trunk Club
tagline: Nordstrom bought the personal stylist that never quite justified the price tag
proximateCause: Nordstrom shut it down after years of failing to make the service profitable
rootCause: once acquired, Trunk Club's high-touch, human-stylist model carried costs that Nordstrom's broader retail business couldn't justify indefinitely, especially as Stitch Fix scaled a cheaper, more automated version of the same idea
timingNote: not primarily a timing issue — personal styling demand was real; the model's underlying economics (human stylists, physical clubhouses) never matched Stitch Fix's more automated cost structure

name: Carwoo
tagline: Tried to make car buying transparent; the dealers who had to cooperate mostly didn't
proximateCause: ran out of funding after raising $16M total
rootCause: Carwoo's reverse-auction model depended on dealer participation and cooperation to work, but dealers had little incentive to compete transparently against each other on price, so the network never reached the density needed to make the product reliably useful
timingNote: not a timing problem — frustration with opaque car pricing was and is real; the constraint was structural resistance from the dealer network the product depended on, not market readiness

name: Webvan
tagline: Promised grocery delivery to 26 cities in 18 months, and the warehouses bankrupted it first
proximateCause: burned through its IPO cash building automated warehouses faster than demand could justify
rootCause: Webvan built capital-intensive automated distribution centers across many cities simultaneously, betting on rapid demand growth that never materialized at dot-com-era prices; the fixed costs of that infrastructure outpaced revenue from actual orders by a huge margin
timingNote: a genuine timing problem — broadband penetration, modern logistics tech, and consumer comfort with online grocery shopping were all roughly a decade away; Webvan built an operationally sound idea for a market and infrastructure environment that didn't exist yet

name: Dot & Bo
tagline: A millennial furniture brand that burned $20M before finding a business model that worked
proximateCause: ran out of venture funding after acquisition talks fell through
rootCause: Dot & Bo's curated, story-driven approach to furniture e-commerce required expensive content production and marketing to compete for the same customers as Wayfair's much larger inventory and ad spend, and it never found a version of the model that was profitable at its funding level
timingNote: not a timing problem — online furniture retail was a real, growing category (Wayfair itself succeeded in it); the failure was a curation-heavy cost structure competing against a scale-first rival

name: Fashism
tagline: Ashton Kutcher's backing couldn't turn outfit votes into revenue
proximateCause: the company couldn't generate enough revenue to sustain operations despite an engaged user base
rootCause: Fashism built real engagement around a fun, low-stakes social feature (vote on my outfit) but never built a monetization layer commensurate with that engagement, so growth in users didn't translate into growth in revenue
timingNote: not a timing issue — the core behavior (seeking outfit feedback) has stayed popular on other platforms; Fashism's specific failure was never solving monetization, not being early or late to the behavior

name: Drizly
tagline: Uber paid $1.1 billion for it, then folded it into Uber Eats three years later
proximateCause: Uber shut it down to fold alcohol delivery directly into the Uber Eats app
rootCause: after acquiring Drizly for $1.1B in 2021, Uber decided a standalone alcohol-delivery app wasn't worth maintaining separately from Uber Eats, especially given the extra regulatory complexity of alcohol delivery across different states; folding it into the main app let Uber keep the category without the standalone overhead
timingNote: not really a market-timing failure — alcohol delivery demand was real and growing; this was a post-acquisition integration decision by the parent company rather than Drizly failing to find a market

name: Proteus Digital Health
tagline: The 'digital pill' pioneer that ran out of cash right as COVID hit
proximateCause: filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after a severe liquidity crisis
rootCause: Proteus depended on a small number of large pharma partnerships (like its collaboration with Otsuka) to fund the years of clinical and regulatory work needed for ingestible sensors; when that partnership scaled back, the company couldn't raise replacement capital in time, and COVID-19 closed the funding window completely
timingNote: a real timing problem — Proteus needed one more funding round to bridge to sustainability, and that round's window closed exactly as COVID-19 froze venture and biotech funding markets in early 2020

name: CareZone
tagline: Sold its best technology to Walmart, then Walmart quietly let the original app die
proximateCause: Walmart discontinued the consumer app after acquiring CareZone's medication-management technology
rootCause: CareZone built genuinely useful medication-management tools, but as a standalone consumer app it couldn't build a durable business around a feature that a company like Walmart could absorb into its own pharmacy ecosystem; selling the technology for around $200M was a good outcome for investors, but it meant the original product had no independent path forward
timingNote: not a timing failure — medication management is a persistent need; the product's fate was tied to being strategically useful to an acquirer rather than being independently sustainable

name: Goldfinch Bio
tagline: $214M and a Gilead partnership weren't enough to survive one disappointing trial readout
proximateCause: couldn't raise additional capital after its lead kidney-disease drug posted underwhelming Phase 2 results
rootCause: Goldfinch built its pipeline around precision treatments for a small number of rare kidney diseases; when its most advanced drug candidate's Phase 2 data came back lukewarm, the company lost its clearest path to a near-term win right as the broader biotech funding environment tightened, leaving no cushion to fund a pivot
timingNote: a timing problem — the Phase 2 disappointment landed during a broader downturn in private biotech funding, so there was no favorable market left to raise a bridge round through

name: Jawbone
tagline: Raised nearly a billion dollars and still couldn't out-ship Fitbit
proximateCause: liquidated its assets after running out of cash and options
rootCause: Jawbone raised enormous amounts of capital relative to its actual product execution, repeatedly shipping late and dealing with product recalls while Fitbit and then Apple Watch captured the wearables market it was trying to lead; commentators called it 'death by overfunding' — the cash cushion let operational problems compound for years instead of forcing a correction
timingNote: not a timing problem — Jawbone was arguably early to wearables; the failure was years of execution problems (late shipping, recalls) that outlasted its enormous funding cushion

name: HealthSpot
tagline: Built a telemedicine kiosk network inside pharmacies, then ran out of cash before it could prove out
proximateCause: ran out of cash and filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, abruptly notifying retail partners it was shutting down within days
rootCause: HealthSpot's kiosk model required expensive hardware deployed and maintained across physical retail locations (Rite Aid, Cleveland Clinic) well before software-based telemedicine had proven a cheaper path to the same outcome; the capital intensity of the hardware rollout outpaced the company's ability to raise enough follow-on funding
timingNote: a real timing problem — HealthSpot bet on hardware kiosks right as smartphone-based telemedicine apps were becoming viable, a far cheaper way to deliver the same remote-visit outcome, which undercut the case for expensive physical kiosks before HealthSpot could scale

name: Zeo
tagline: Measured your sleep stages with real EEG tech, in a headband nobody wanted to wear to bed
proximateCause: the business model didn't generate enough margin to sustain the company
rootCause: Zeo's founder pointed to a 'suboptimal profit margin' business model combined with a physically invasive headband device and a clunky requirement to manually log data on a website — friction that limited how many people would actually adopt and keep using a sleep tracker in this form factor
timingNote: a timing problem in the sense that Zeo arrived years before comfortable, unobtrusive sleep tracking (built into watches and rings) became possible; the underlying headband-EEG approach was never going to reach mass comfort no matter how long Zeo waited

name: Arivale
tagline: Personalized wellness backed by real genomics data, priced out of reach of the people it wanted to help
proximateCause: shut down abruptly, saying the cost of running the service exceeded what customers could pay
rootCause: Arivale's coaching was built on genuinely rigorous genetic, blood, and microbiome testing, but that same rigor made the direct-to-consumer cost structure unsustainable — the tests needed to power each customer's personalized plan cost more than a consumer subscription business could recover
timingNote: not a timing problem — personalized wellness coaching remains in demand; the failure was a cost structure (expensive lab testing per customer) that a direct-to-consumer subscription price could never cover

name: LendUp
tagline: Marketed itself as the ethical alternative to payday loans, then got shut down for deceptive lending
proximateCause: the CFPB ordered it to stop making new loans and fined it for repeated deceptive practices
rootCause: LendUp built its brand around a 'ladder' that promised responsible borrowers access to larger loans at better rates, but regulators found that promise didn't hold for tens of thousands of customers in practice; a 2016 CFPB order followed by continued violations led to a second, terminal enforcement action in 2021 that ended its ability to lend at all
timingNote: not a timing problem — subprime lending demand was constant throughout; the failure was a sustained gap between LendUp's marketed promise and its actual practices, which regulators eventually treated as a pattern rather than a one-time violation

name: Clarity Money
tagline: Goldman Sachs bought it, borrowed its best ideas for Marcus, then closed the original app
proximateCause: Goldman Sachs wound the app down after migrating its most-used features into its own Marcus Insights product
rootCause: once Goldman acquired Clarity Money in 2018, the app's long-term fate depended on Goldman's own consumer-banking strategy rather than the product's independent traction; Goldman ultimately decided to fold the best ideas into its own Marcus brand instead of continuing to run a separately branded app, ending Clarity Money's existence
timingNote: not a timing failure by Clarity Money's own product-market fit — it was a strategic decision by its acquirer to consolidate features under its own brand, which can happen to any acquired app whose parent company reprioritizes

name: Isentium
tagline: Built the sentiment-analysis engine Bloomberg's terminal used, until Bloomberg built its own
proximateCause: lost its primary distribution channel when Bloomberg ended their partnership and launched a competing in-house app
rootCause: Isentium's business depended heavily on its integration into the Bloomberg Terminal to reach financial customers; once Bloomberg decided the sentiment-analysis feature was valuable enough to build in-house rather than license, Isentium lost its main distribution channel, and a costly IP lawsuit against Bloomberg drained resources without winning back that access
timingNote: not a timing problem — social-sentiment trading signals remained a real product category; the failure was structural dependence on a single distribution partner who had every incentive to eventually build the feature itself

name: Bitpass
tagline: Tried to make small online payments work years before anyone would pay for small online payments
proximateCause: shut down and closed all customer accounts after concluding the business wasn't viable
rootCause: Bitpass explicitly cited competition from Google Checkout, launched the same year, as undermining its micropayments system; a free, general-purpose payment option from a company with Google's reach and distribution made a standalone micropayments-specific startup redundant almost overnight
timingNote: a timing problem — Bitpass was pursuing a real need (small digital-content payments) years before that need had a viable large-scale solution, and when a well-resourced entrant (Google) finally addressed it, a small independent player couldn't compete on distribution

name: Lytro
tagline: Reinvented the camera at the sensor level, and still lost to the phone in your pocket
proximateCause: shut down after failing to build a sustainable market for its light-field cameras
rootCause: Lytro's light-field sensor technology was a genuine computational-photography breakthrough, but neither its consumer cameras nor its later pivot to professional and VR cameras found a market big enough to justify the hardware's cost; meanwhile smartphone cameras absorbed computational photography features (like depth-of-field effects) through software, closing the gap Lytro's hardware was built to fill
timingNote: a timing problem — Lytro's core insight (compute depth and focus after the shot) turned out to be right, but smartphones delivered a software version of that insight to billions of people before Lytro's specialized hardware could find a large enough market of its own

name: Aria Insights
tagline: Rebranded from hardware to data days before shutting down entirely
proximateCause: shut down abruptly, just two months after rebranding from CyPhy Works to focus on drone data instead of drone hardware
rootCause: as CyPhy Works, the company built tethered industrial drones but couldn't build a hardware business competitive with DJI's manufacturing scale; the last-minute pivot to a data/analytics business model came too late to raise the funding needed to make that transition, and the company ran out of runway almost immediately after rebranding
timingNote: a timing problem in its final act — the strategic pivot to a data business might have been the right long-term direction, but it happened too late relative to the company's remaining cash to give the new model a real chance to prove itself

name: Maple
tagline: Vertically integrated the entire meal-delivery chain, and still lost money on every meal
proximateCause: sold its technology and team to European rival Deliveroo rather than continue operating independently
rootCause: Maple owned its own kitchens, delivery fleet, and app to control quality end-to-end, but that vertical integration meant carrying the full fixed costs of restaurant-grade food production without restaurant-scale volume; the company was reportedly losing money on every meal it delivered, and rather than keep funding that gap, it sold its assets to Deliveroo and its team relocated to London
timingNote: not a timing problem — food delivery was a booming, well-timed category; the failure was a cost structure (owning the entire kitchen-to-doorstep chain) that couldn't reach profitability at the volumes Maple achieved

name: Munchery
tagline: Chef-prepared meals at scale, undone by aggressive expansion it couldn't afford
proximateCause: shut down abruptly and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after running out of cash
rootCause: Munchery expanded into new cities faster than it could establish efficient kitchen and delivery operations in each one, and increasing competition made it harder to acquire new customers cheaply enough to offset that expansion cost; by the time it shut down it owed millions to vendors and gift-card-holding customers it couldn't pay back
timingNote: not a timing problem — meal delivery was a real, growing category (competitors survived); the failure was expanding faster than the unit economics in each new market could support

name: Cafe X
tagline: Robot baristas were a great demo and a hard sell at street-level foot traffic
proximateCause: closed its downtown storefront locations, then its airport locations, as pandemic foot traffic collapsed
rootCause: Cafe X's downtown San Francisco locations were explicitly described by its own CEO as running 'prototype' machines meant to learn about customer behavior rather than a proven profitable format; when the company pivoted to airport locations to find a better foot-traffic model, the COVID-19 collapse in air travel removed that foot traffic before the pivot could be judged on its own terms
timingNote: a real timing problem in its final act — the pivot to airport kiosks might have found a workable niche, but the pandemic's collapse in air travel hit right as that new bet was being placed

name: NewsTilt
tagline: A platform to make journalists into entrepreneurs, launched with no journalists and no readers on either side
proximateCause: shut down about two months after launch after failing to attract either journalists or an audience
rootCause: NewsTilt tried to build a marketplace connecting journalists with an audience, but launched hoping supply and demand would meet rather than having built either side first; founder Paul Biggar later wrote that neither co-founder had a journalism background or real passion for the idea, and the company burned through its Y Combinator funding chasing a two-sided market that never formed
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” the failure was fundamental market design (a two-sided marketplace with neither side present at launch) and founder-market fit, not something more time would have fixed

name: Wickr
tagline: Built one of the first mainstream encrypted messengers, then Amazon quietly euthanized the consumer version
proximateCause: AWS shut down the free consumer app, Wickr Me, on December 31, 2023, after acquiring Wickr in 2021
rootCause: after Amazon Web Services acquired Wickr in 2021, it kept investing in the enterprise- and government-focused Wickr/AWS Wickr products but decided the free consumer messaging app no longer fit its business priorities; new signups were cut off at the end of 2022 and the app was fully shut down a year later so AWS could concentrate on business and public-sector customers instead
timingNote: not a market-timing failure â€” encrypted messaging remained in high demand throughout (Signal and WhatsApp both grew); this was an acquirer's strategic choice to deprioritize a free consumer product, not the market rejecting it

name: Ahalife
tagline: A curated luxury marketplace that survived an IPO and a leadership shakeup, but not the cost of acquiring customers
proximateCause: the company quietly stopped operating around 2020 after years of restructuring, and is listed as 'Dead' by CB Insights
rootCause: AHAlife spent heavily on marketing to compete for high-end shoppers against Amazon and dedicated luxury e-commerce players, and after a 2016 ASX listing it went through a 2017 restructuring in which both co-founders left their executive roles; the site kept limping along with service and fulfillment problems (an expired SSL certificate, unresolved customer orders) before going dark around 2020 without a formal shutdown announcement
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” curated luxury e-commerce was and is a viable category (Moda Operandi and others succeeded in it); AHAlife's failure was a marketing-cost structure and leadership instability that a niche audience couldn't sustain

name: Gowalla
tagline: Lost the location check-in war to Foursquare, then got bought by Facebook just for the team
proximateCause: Facebook acquired Gowalla in December 2011 purely for its team, and shut the product down by March 2012
rootCause: Gowalla and Foursquare fought head-to-head for the location-based check-in market through 2010-2011, and Foursquare pulled decisively ahead in users and brand recognition; Facebook's acquisition was explicitly an acqui-hire for the founders' design and engineering talent rather than a purchase of Gowalla's technology or user base, so the product itself was wound down within three months
timingNote: a network-effects timing loss more than a pure market-timing one â€” Gowalla and Foursquare launched into the same window, but Foursquare won the scale race, and once one player pulled ahead in a winner-take-most category the also-ran had no independent path forward

name: Vine
tagline: Invented six-second video stardom, then its own parent company starved it of the tools to compete
proximateCause: Twitter announced in October 2016 it would shut down the Vine app, folding it down completely by January 2017
rootCause: Twitter acquired Vine before launch in 2012 but never invested enough in creator monetization or platform development to keep pace once Instagram (adding video in 2013) and Snapchat drew away both users and creators; facing its own financial pressure and an unsuccessful search for a buyer for the whole company, Twitter cut Vine as part of a broader round of layoffs rather than keep funding a product it had let stagnate
timingNote: a real timing failure â€” Vine had first-mover advantage in short-form video, but Twitter's years of underinvestment let Instagram and Snapchat catch up and overtake it before Twitter finally acted, so by the time it needed to compete, the moment for standalone short video had already passed to rivals

name: 99dresses
tagline: A teenage founder's viral closet-swap app that couldn't make its US relaunch stick
proximateCause: shut down in 2014 after a US relaunch failed to replicate the engagement of its original Australian user base
rootCause: 99dresses built a loyal following in Australia around swapping secondhand clothes using an in-app credit currency, but when 19-year-old founder Nikki Durkin moved the company to San Francisco and rebuilt it as a US-first mobile product, American users didn't adopt the virtual-currency swapping mechanic the way Australian users had, and the company burned through its funding without finding the same traction in the new market
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” clothing swap and resale later became a large category (Poshmark, ThredUp); 99dresses' failure was a market-fit and localization problem when it tried to transplant an Australia-specific mechanic to US users, not a market that wasn't ready

name: Kozmo.com
tagline: Promised free one-hour delivery of almost anything, and free was exactly the problem
proximateCause: shut down all operations in April 2001 after burning through its funding without ever turning a profit
rootCause: Kozmo built an entire courier and warehouse infrastructure to deliver small items like videos and snacks with no delivery fee and no minimum order size, so it was structurally paying more per delivery than many orders were worth; when the dot-com crash cut off the additional venture capital the model depended on, there was no way to keep subsidizing every order and the company folded, laying off nearly 1,100 employees at once
timingNote: a genuine timing problem in the sense that broadband, smartphone logistics, and gig-economy delivery labor were all a decade away, but the core issue ran deeper than timing â€” the free-delivery-of-anything model didn't have viable unit economics at any point without those later tools

name: GetGlue
tagline: Gamified checking in to TV shows, then got sold, renamed, and shut down within about a year
proximateCause: i.TV, which had acquired GetGlue and relaunched it as TVtag, shut the service down entirely on January 1, 2015
rootCause: GetGlue's core loop of checking in to TV shows and collecting virtual stickers never became a habit for enough viewers as streaming fragmented the shared live-TV moment it depended on; i.TV acquired the struggling service in November 2013, rebranded it as TVtag, and after roughly a year of trying to make the concept work under new ownership, decided to redirect its resources elsewhere and pulled the plug
timingNote: a timing problem â€” social TV check-ins made more sense in an era of appointment live television, and by the time GetGlue/TVtag needed a mass audience, on-demand and streaming viewing habits had already fragmented the 'watching together' moment the product was built around

name: Juicero
tagline: A $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that a Bloomberg reporter proved you could squeeze by hand
proximateCause: shut down in September 2017 after a Bloomberg video showed its proprietary juice packs could be squeezed by hand nearly as effectively as by the machine
rootCause: Juicero built an internet-connected press using DRM-locked produce packs that cost $400 (later $700), positioning itself as sophisticated hardware; when Bloomberg demonstrated in April 2017 that consumers could get nearly identical juice by hand-squeezing the packs, it undercut the entire premise of needing an expensive machine and turned the company into a punchline, and the company â€” already reportedly losing about $4 million a month building out nationwide distribution â€” never recovered
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” the failure was a fundamental product-value mismatch (an expensive machine solving a problem hands could solve for free), not a market that wasn't ready

name: Grooveshark
tagline: Let anyone upload music for free, then got legislated and litigated out of existence
proximateCause: shut down permanently on April 30, 2015, as part of a settlement with major record labels UMG, Sony, and Warner
rootCause: Grooveshark's core product let users upload and stream music freely without licensing agreements from labels, which powered explosive early growth (35 million users at its peak) but also constituted the copyright infringement labels sued over starting in 2011; facing a trial with potential damages of up to $736 million, the company agreed to shut down entirely, wipe its music library, hand over its IP, and pay $50 million rather than risk a larger judgment
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” the failure was structural and legal from day one: building a music platform on unlicensed user uploads was always going to collide with copyright law once it got big enough for labels to sue

name: Pulse
tagline: A slick news reader LinkedIn paid $90M for, then folded into a feature nobody asked to keep separate
proximateCause: LinkedIn officially discontinued the standalone Pulse app on May 31, 2017
rootCause: LinkedIn acquired Pulse for $90 million in 2013 to add news-reading habits to its platform, first replacing its own LinkedIn Today feature with it and later trying a redesigned personalized-news app; neither version became central enough to LinkedIn's strategy, and the company eventually folded Pulse's remaining function into the main site's 'Articles' publishing feature, retiring the standalone app entirely
timingNote: not really a market-timing failure â€” this was an acquirer absorbing and eventually discontinuing a standalone product as its own strategy evolved, not Pulse failing to find a market on its own

name: Ecomom
tagline: An eco-friendly baby products retailer undone by a discount policy that lost money on every sale
proximateCause: wound down due to financial insolvency in early 2013, shortly after founder and CEO Jody Sherman's death
rootCause: Ecomom adopted an uncapped 50%-off discount policy that let repeat customers buy below cost indefinitely, so growth in orders actively drained cash rather than building revenue; CEO Jody Sherman, by his own team's account, didn't understand the resulting margin problem, and after raising over $12M the 28-person startup ran out of cash with no one able to account for where it had gone
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” the failure was financial mismanagement (a discount structure that guaranteed losses) rather than a market that wasn't ready for eco-friendly baby products

name: Fancy
tagline: A Pinterest-for-shopping platform that burned through $100M chasing Amazon and Shopify's turf
proximateCause: operations gradually wound down and the company effectively closed by October 2020 after years of shrinking margins and no path to profitability
rootCause: Fancy built a social discovery and shopping platform that let users curate and buy from a visually driven catalog, but its gross margins nearly halved between 2018 and 2019 as it competed for the same merchants and shoppers as much larger, better-resourced platforms like Shopify and Amazon; despite raising and spending roughly $100 million, and bringing in a new CEO in 2019 to try to reinvent the brand, the company couldn't find a profitable version of the model before it ran out of runway
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” social/curated e-commerce had real proof points elsewhere; Fancy's failure was a margin and competitive-positioning problem against much larger platforms, not a market that wasn't ready

name: Combatant Gentlemen
tagline: Promised sharp, affordable suits by mail, then buckled under its own growth and unfulfilled orders
proximateCause: filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2018 after quality-control problems, unfulfilled orders, and mounting customer-service complaints piled up
rootCause: Combatant Gentlemen scaled its direct-to-consumer menswear business quickly, but rapid growth outpaced its ability to maintain product quality and reliably fulfill orders; as complaints about unfulfilled orders and poor customer service accumulated, the resulting reputational damage and financial strain forced the third-generation-tailor-founded company into bankruptcy
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” affordable direct-to-consumer menswear was and remained a viable category; the failure was operational, scaling faster than the company's fulfillment and quality processes could support

name: Nasty Gal
tagline: The eBay-store-turned-fashion-unicorn that couldn't survive its own overexpansion
proximateCause: filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in November 2016 after years of executive turnover and slowing sales, with its assets sold off in a bankruptcy auction
rootCause: Nasty Gal expanded rapidly from a scrappy eBay vintage-resale shop into a venture-backed fast-fashion brand, opening physical stores and burning through cash on marketing and leadership changes (including multiple CEO transitions) faster than its sales could support; when growth slowed, the company couldn't refinance its way out and filed for bankruptcy, with British fast-fashion retailer Boohoo winning the $20 million stalking-horse bid for its brand and customer data in a court-approved sale that closed in February 2017
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” fast-fashion e-commerce was thriving throughout this period (ASOS and Boohoo itself both succeeded); Nasty Gal's failure was a self-inflicted scaling and management problem, not a market that wasn't ready

name: Beepi
tagline: Promised to reinvent buying a used car peer-to-peer, then burned $7M a month getting there
proximateCause: shut down operations outside California in December 2016 after a planned merger with Fair.com collapsed, and wound down entirely by early 2017 through an assignment for the benefit of creditors
rootCause: Beepi built a capital-intensive operation â€” buying, inspecting, reconditioning, and shipping used cars peer-to-peer â€” while spending around $7 million a month, much of it on inflated salaries and other non-essential costs; when it couldn't raise a new round on those terms, a planned sale to Fair.com fell apart, a follow-up deal with a California dealer group also fell through, and the company had no path left but to liquidate its remaining assets to repay creditors
timingNote: not a timing problem â€” peer-to-peer and online used-car sales later became a large, successful category (Carvana, Vroom); Beepi's failure was an unsustainable burn rate and operational cost structure, not a market that wasn't ready

name: Pets.com
tagline: The sock-puppet mascot became more famous than the unprofitable business underneath it
proximateCause: announced on November 7, 2000 that it would stop taking orders and liquidate, going from IPO to shutdown in 268 days
rootCause: Pets.com sold heavy, low-margin pet supplies like litter and food below cost while absorbing expensive shipping itself, and it spent aggressively on brand marketing (a Super Bowl ad, the Macy's Parade) to build awareness faster than its unit economics could support; when the dot-com funding market collapsed in 2000, there was no more capital to keep subsidizing every order, and there was no profitable business underneath the marketing
timingNote: a genuine timing problem â€” the infrastructure Pets.com needed (cheap fulfillment logistics, higher broadband and e-commerce adoption) arrived roughly a decade later and enabled companies like Chewy to succeed with a similar premise

name: Nuzzel
tagline: A personalized Twitter news feed that got acquired twice and folded both times
proximateCause: Twitter acquired Scroll, which owned Nuzzel, in May 2021 and decided to shut Nuzzel down rather than keep operating it independently.
rootCause: Nuzzel had already been acquired once, by ad-blocking subscription startup Scroll in 2019, which ran it with what insiders called 'quick fixes and duct tape' rather than real investment. When Twitter acquired Scroll in 2021 to build its own subscription news product, its engineers concluded that reaching the scale needed to integrate Nuzzel into Twitter would mean rebuilding it from scratch, so it was simpler to shut the standalone app down and absorb the personalized-newsfeed concept into Twitter's own roadmap.
timingNote: Not really a timing problem — Nuzzel was a two-time acquisition target that never found an independent business model; each new owner treated it as a feature to be absorbed rather than a product worth keeping alive.

name: Rockmelt
tagline: The social browser Yahoo bought for its team, then killed within weeks
proximateCause: Yahoo acquired Rockmelt in August 2013 and shut down all of its apps and its browser by the end of that month.
rootCause: Rockmelt's original pitch — a browser built around Facebook and Twitter feeds — never found mass adoption, reaching only about 4 million registrations by late 2012. The team abandoned the browser and pivoted to a Pinterest-style mobile content-discovery app instead, which also failed to gain traction. Yahoo's roughly $60-70M acquisition was aimed mainly at the team and technology, and came with an immediate decision to kill the consumer-facing products.
timingNote: A timing problem — Rockmelt bet on the browser as the place to layer social features right as Chrome was consolidating the browser market and social discovery was shifting to native apps and feeds, leaving little room for a niche browser.

name: Divshot
tagline: An HTML5 hosting startup Google bought for its team and shut down two months later
proximateCause: Google acquired Divshot's team and technology in October 2015 and shut the standalone product down two months later, on December 14, 2015.
rootCause: Divshot built an HTML5 web-app hosting and builder platform but couldn't grow it into a sustainable standalone business against much larger, better-funded hosting competitors. Google acquired it purely to bring the team onto the Firebase project — its eleventh acquisition that year — and had no interest in keeping the Divshot product itself running, so it set a hard shutdown date for existing customers.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem — it was a small niche tool absorbed into a much bigger platform (Firebase) as an acquihire rather than a company that missed a market window.

name: Thalmic Labs
tagline: From gesture-control armbands to smart glasses, killed a month after Google bought the company
proximateCause: Google acquired Thalmic Labs (by then rebranded North) in mid-2020 and discontinued its Focals smart glasses within a month of the deal closing.
rootCause: Thalmic's original Myo gesture-control armband never found a mainstream use case, so the company pivoted entirely to smart glasses under the North brand. Focals also failed to gain a wide audience, and when Google bought North in June 2020 for a reported ~£145M — mainly for its optics and display talent — it immediately wound down Focals 1.0 and cancelled the unreleased Focals 2.0, offering refunds to customers.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem — smart-glasses hardware was still years from consumer-market fit, and the company burned through two full product pivots (Myo, then Focals) trying to find one before running out of runway as an independent company.

name: Milk
tagline: Kevin Rose's app lab that treated its own product as a disposable experiment
proximateCause: Milk shut down its only shipped product, the Oink rating app, after just a few months, and its founding team was acqui-hired by Google.
rootCause: Kevin Rose's app studio Milk built Oink, a place-and-dish rating app, as an explicit 'test' concept rather than a committed product. When it failed to gain traction, Milk's entire product team — including Rose — was hired away by Google in a deal reportedly worth $15-30M, ending Milk as an independent company just months after Oink launched.
timingNote: Not really a timing failure — the company treated its own product as disposable from the start, framing Oink explicitly as a test rather than committing to iterate on it.

name: GeoCities
tagline: The web's first mass homesteading platform, left to rot by Yahoo for a decade
proximateCause: Yahoo formally shut down GeoCities on October 26, 2009, deleting the personal home pages of users who hadn't migrated to paid Yahoo Web Hosting.
rootCause: Yahoo bought GeoCities for over $3 billion at the height of the dot-com boom but never modernized or monetized its free personal-homepage model. As MySpace, Blogger and other social and blogging platforms overtook it through the mid-2000s, Yahoo let the product stagnate for years before announcing the shutdown in April 2009 and pulling the plug that October.
timingNote: A pure timing failure — GeoCities' static-page hosting model was overtaken by the shift to social networking and blogging, and its acquirer sat on the asset for a decade without adapting it to the new web.

name: Hot Potato
tagline: A Foursquare rival Facebook bought for the team and deleted within a month
proximateCause: Facebook acquired Hot Potato in July 2010 for its engineering team and shut down the check-in service about a month later, deleting all user data.
rootCause: Hot Potato was a small check-in and social-activity startup competing directly with the fast-growing Foursquare. Rather than try to out-scale that competition, Facebook bought the eight-person team for roughly $10M purely for talent, following its typical acqui-hire pattern of that era, with no plan to keep operating the product.
timingNote: A timing and competitive problem more than anything — it launched right as Foursquare was becoming the dominant check-in app, leaving little room for a similarly-scoped rival to build independent scale before being swallowed for its team.

name: Lot18
tagline: A wine flash-sale site that pivoted for a decade before finally closing
proximateCause: After years of downsizing, pivots away from flash sales, and closing its foreign operations, Lot18 wound down completely by 2023.
rootCause: Lot18 raised roughly $50M to run flash sales on wine and gourmet food, but state-by-state alcohol shipping laws, thin margins on discounted wine, and heavy competition made the model unsustainable. It went through multiple rounds of layoffs starting in 2012, closed its UK operation that same year, and pivoted to a subscription model, but never returned to its earlier scale before finally closing.
timingNote: Less a timing problem than a structural one — U.S. alcohol regulation and thin retail margins made wine flash sales a persistently hard business, not a market that briefly closed on Lot18.

name: Teespring
tagline: The custom-apparel unicorn that collapsed overnight after rebranding to Spring
proximateCause: Spring (formerly Teespring) collapsed without warning at the start of 2023, laying off its entire staff overnight.
rootCause: After rebranding from Teespring to Spring and shutting its only owned production facility in Kentucky in late 2022 in favor of third-party print partners, the company's fulfillment quality and reliability slipped. Its valuation reportedly fell from around $650M to roughly $11M, and it was hit with lawsuits from vendors and partners over more than $1.5M in unpaid bills before shutting down entirely.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing issue — it was a self-inflicted operational collapse (outsourcing production, cash problems, unpaid vendors) rather than a market that moved on.

name: Plum District
tagline: A daily-deals site for moms that outlasted the deal-fatigue collapse by years, barely
proximateCause: Plum District's independent operations ended when its website was acquired and merged into Coupon Lawn in July 2020.
rootCause: Plum District built a hyperlocal daily-deals site targeted at mothers, but faced heavy competition from Groupon and LivingSocial in the same deal-fatigue-prone category. The company ran through repeated layoffs starting in 2012, shrank from a peak of 27 markets to a fraction of that, and was never able to reach profitability before its remaining assets were absorbed by a discount-code aggregator years later.
timingNote: A timing problem — Plum District rode the daily-deals boom of 2010-2012 right as consumer deal fatigue set in and the category itself began collapsing industry-wide, not just for Plum District.

name: Whisper
tagline: The anonymous confession app that outran regulators until it couldn't
proximateCause: Whisper was permanently discontinued after years of repeated app-store bans tied to child-safety and predator concerns.
rootCause: Once valued near $200M, Whisper built its identity around fully anonymous confession-style posting, which made it a magnet for predatory behavior and abuse. It was repeatedly pulled from and reinstated to the Apple and Google app stores between 2022 and 2025 amid platform and institutional bans — including a 2024 UNC university-system ban alongside similar anonymous apps — before finally disappearing for good.
timingNote: Not a timing problem so much as a trust-and-safety problem baked into its core anonymity feature, which regulators, platforms and institutions increasingly refused to tolerate as scrutiny of anonymous apps grew.

name: Yelp Deals
tagline: Yelp's daily-deals product, kept on life support a decade past the category's collapse
proximateCause: Yelp fully discontinued its Deals and Gift Certificates products in late 2024, removing them from the platform by December 9, 2024.
rootCause: Yelp Deals launched during the daily-deals boom to compete with Groupon and LivingSocial, but businesses and consumers moved away from voucher-style discounting well before Yelp finally wound the feature down. Yelp phased it out gradually — closing new-deal creation in October 2024, ending purchases later that month, and pulling the remaining interface in December — pointing businesses instead to newer ad-based tools.
timingNote: A timing problem — deal fatigue had already killed most of the daily-deals category by the mid-2010s, and Yelp simply kept a fading feature alive far longer than the market wanted before formally retiring it.

name: Dyson's EV Project
tagline: A £500M electric car that James Dyson killed rather than ship at a loss
proximateCause: Dyson cancelled its electric vehicle program outright in October 2019 without ever bringing a car to market.
rootCause: Dyson spent roughly £500M actually building prototypes of a three-row electric SUV, planning to manufacture in Singapore for a 2021 launch. The company concluded the vehicle could not be made commercially viable — it could not find a buyer for the completed design, and the economics of low-volume EV manufacturing against Tesla and established automakers didn't work even for a company with deep engineering resources.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem — Dyson entered EV development years after Tesla had already established scale advantages and a charging and software ecosystem, making it very hard for a newcomer, however well-funded, to compete on unit economics.

name: Udacity Blitz
tagline: Udacity's freelance-marketplace side project, abandoned after a year
proximateCause: Udacity wound down its Blitz freelance-marketplace program in November 2017, ending new freelance project engagements.
rootCause: Blitz let companies hire teams of Udacity-trained Nanodegree graduates as freelancers, with Udacity taking a 5-10% cut of each project. The extension never became more than a small side program next to Udacity's core education and career-services business, and after about a year Udacity redirected its resources into its Career Resource Center and hiring partnerships instead of running its own freelance marketplace.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — it was a narrow adjacent-market experiment that Udacity abandoned quickly once it decided the freelance-marketplace business wasn't core to its education mission.

name: Hello
tagline: A beautifully-designed sleep tracker that died when a Fitbit deal fell through
proximateCause: Hello Inc. shut down in June 2017 after acquisition talks with Fitbit fell through, laying off most staff the same day.
rootCause: Hello built the Sense sleep tracker, a well-reviewed but commercially underwhelming hardware product that depended entirely on Hello's own cloud infrastructure to function. When the company couldn't raise further funding or find a buyer beyond a failed Fitbit deal, founder James Proud announced the shutdown, and existing Sense devices became effectively useless within about two months once the backing servers went dark.
timingNote: A timing and competitive problem — Sense arrived as Fitbit and Apple Watch were consolidating the broader wearables and sleep-tracking market, leaving little independent room for single-purpose sleep hardware that depended on continuous cloud support.

name: Better Place
tagline: An $850M bet on swappable EV batteries that only one automaker ever joined
proximateCause: Better Place filed for bankruptcy in Israel on May 26, 2013, after burning through its funding without reaching viable scale.
rootCause: Better Place built an expensive network of battery-swap stations for electric vehicles, betting automakers would adopt its swappable-battery standard. Only Renault ever signed on, and just 950 cars using the system were ever sold, while the company lost $812M in its final year and would have needed another $500M and four more years to break even — money it could no longer raise. Its bankrupt assets were later sold off for a fraction of the capital invested.
timingNote: A genuine timing problem — Better Place bet on a specific technical solution (battery swapping) to EV range anxiety right as battery energy density and charging infrastructure were rapidly improving, and the market ultimately standardized on plug-in charging instead, stranding its entire infrastructure investment.

name: Loyal3
tagline: The commission-free brokerage that was ahead of Robinhood, and lost to it anyway
proximateCause: Loyal3 shut down its brokerage service effective May 22, 2017, transferring client accounts to FolioFirst.
rootCause: Loyal3 pioneered commission-free stock trading years before Robinhood made the model mainstream, letting users buy fractional shares for as little as $10 with no fees, including access to select company IPOs. But it never reached the scale or venture backing that Robinhood achieved once that competitor entered the same space, and it ultimately closed down, pushing its users to a paid alternative that charged $5/month.
timingNote: A timing problem — Loyal3 was arguably ahead of its time on commission-free trading but couldn't sustain the model on its own before a better-funded competitor captured the category it had helped pioneer.

name: Wishbone
tagline: A teen polling app undone by two data breaches it never fixed the cause of
proximateCause: Wishbone was discontinued after suffering a second, much larger data breach in early 2020 that exposed the personal records of more than 40 million users.
rootCause: The teen polling app had already been breached once in 2017, exposing 2.2 million emails and phone numbers, but failed to fix its underlying security practices. In January 2020 a hacker calling themselves 'ShinyHunters' stole and leaked data — usernames, emails, full names, phone numbers, birthdates and hashed passwords — for over 40 million accounts, and the app was effectively abandoned in the aftermath.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — it was a trust failure. Repeated security lapses destroyed user confidence in an app whose core appeal, casual polling with friends, depended on being a safe, low-stakes place to share preferences.

name: Lily Robotics
tagline: $34M in drone pre-orders, zero drones shipped, one false-advertising lawsuit
proximateCause: Lily Robotics shut down in January 2017 and filed for bankruptcy the following month, after taking $34M in customer pre-orders without ever shipping a single drone.
rootCause: Lily promoted its self-flying camera drone with a viral 2015 launch video that the San Francisco District Attorney later alleged used footage from competitors' drones fitted with GoPro and DJI cameras, rather than Lily's actual prototype. After nearly two years and 60,000 pre-orders totaling $34M with no shipped product, the company announced its shutdown the same day it learned of the DA's false-advertising lawsuit, then filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy while attempting to refund customers.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — a hardware execution and integrity failure. The company oversold its technical progress publicly for years longer than its actual engineering could support.

name: Lantern
tagline: A CBT mental-health app that spread itself across three buyers and satisfied none
proximateCause: Lantern wound down its customer-facing operations in July 2018 after two prospective acquisition deals fell through.
rootCause: Lantern offered a subscription CBT-based mental-health app, around $50/month, aimed at consumers, employers and health-plan payers simultaneously. Spreading itself across three different buyer types at once diluted its execution and sales focus, and when it couldn't close an acquisition to keep the business funded, it laid off roughly 25 staff and ended paid service by the end of 2018. Its technology was later licensed to Spring Health.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing issue — the CEO attributed the failure mainly to trying to serve too many customer segments (consumer, employer and payer) at once, which undermined focused execution rather than a shift in market conditions.

name: Call9
tagline: On-site paramedics for nursing homes, priced out of its own business model
proximateCause: Call9 shut down most of its operations in mid-2019 after failing to raise additional venture funding.
rootCause: Call9 placed paramedics on-site inside skilled nursing facilities, connected via iPad to remote physicians, aiming to cut unnecessary ER visits from nursing-home residents. Despite $34M raised from investors including Index Ventures, Y Combinator and Anne Wojcicki, the capital-intensive, staff-heavy model never reached the scale needed to become self-sustaining, and when new funding didn't materialize the company laid off about 100 employees and ceased most operations.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — a unit-economics problem. Embedding paid clinical staff at every partner facility made the model expensive to scale regardless of market timing.

name: Wepay
tagline: A payments pioneer JPMorgan bought, then quietly wound down seven years later
proximateCause: JPMorgan Chase discontinued WePay, abruptly cutting off many long-standing business customers starting in 2024 before fully sunsetting the service.
rootCause: JPMorgan acquired WePay in 2017 to power payments for small platforms and marketplaces, but the bank ultimately decided the business no longer fit its strategy. Starting around January 2024 it stopped supporting many WePay clients, then set a formal wind-down timeline: new payments stopped by July 1, 2024, support ended September 29, 2024, and remaining account functions like deposits, refunds and chargebacks closed out by January 10, 2025.
timingNote: Not a market-timing failure — it was a strategic decision by its acquirer, JPMorgan, to exit a business line years after buying it, unrelated to WePay's original product-market fit.

name: Zulily
tagline: The flash-sale pioneer that outlived two owners before finally liquidating
proximateCause: Zulily ceased operations entirely on December 22, 2023, just seven months after being sold to private-equity firm Regent.
rootCause: Zulily pioneered flash-sale e-commerce for moms' and kids' goods and was acquired by QVC-parent Qurate Retail in 2015, but the flash-sale model steadily lost ground to Amazon's everyday-low-price convenience. Sales kept declining under Qurate, which sold Zulily to Regent in May 2023, and just months later, facing a 17% revenue drop and a $43M quarterly operating loss, Zulily wound down completely, laying off about 850 employees and liquidating its assets.
timingNote: A timing problem in the sense that the flash-sale category itself had been declining for years before Zulily's final collapse — its last owners inherited a business already past its peak rather than one that failed suddenly.

name: Curb Food
tagline: A Stockholm robot-run kitchen chain that couldn't out-cook the ghost-kitchen crash.
proximateCause: Ceased all operations in December 2022 after burning through tens of millions in funding on unmanned kitchen hardware.
rootCause: Curb Food built a network of unmanned, robot-operated 'ghost kitchens' across Stockholm, betting that automation could make delivery-only restaurants profitable at scale. But the pandemic-era delivery boom that justified dark-kitchen economics faded quickly once dine-in reopened, and the fixed costs of running automated kitchen hardware didn't shrink with falling order volumes. Despite raising roughly €23M from investors, the company could not find a path to profitability and wound down in December 2022, joining a wave of European ghost-kitchen startups that collapsed the same year.
timingNote: This was fundamentally a timing problem: Curb Food scaled hardware-heavy dark kitchens right as the pandemic delivery surge that created ghost-kitchen demand reversed, leaving it with expensive infrastructure and shrinking order volumes.

name: ContextLogic
tagline: The bargain-bin shopping app that couldn't outrun its own reputation for junk.
proximateCause: Revenue collapsed to a fraction of its peak, and in 2024 ContextLogic sold off the entire Wish platform and its operating assets to Qoo10 rather than keep running it.
rootCause: Wish built its business on ultra-cheap, mostly China-sourced goods with weeks-long shipping times, which drove early growth but bred a reputation for counterfeit and low-quality merchandise as competitors like Amazon and Temu offered faster, more reliable alternatives. Trust and repeat usage collapsed: Q1 2024 revenue fell 63% year-over-year to $36 million, and cash flow turned deeply negative. With no viable turnaround plan, ContextLogic's board pursued a sale rather than continue funding losses, closing the sale of Wish's assets to Singapore's Qoo10 in April 2024 for roughly 1% of the company's former valuation.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem — Wish had a decade to build trust and failed, while faster-shipping, curated rivals like Temu (which launched later, in 2022) ate its market with a similar low-price model executed better.

name: Homejoy
tagline: The on-demand cleaning unicorn hopeful that gig-worker lawsuits swept away.
proximateCause: Shut down abruptly on July 31, 2015, with CEO Adora Cheung citing four pending worker-misclassification lawsuits as the deciding factor.
rootCause: Homejoy classified its home cleaners as independent contractors, which let it avoid providing benefits and kept costs low, but this became a legal liability once several class-action suits challenged that classification following a California Labor Commissioner ruling that an Uber driver was an employee. The lawsuits made it too risky for investors to fund another round in the on-demand-labor space, and Homejoy was also losing a bruising customer-retention battle to well-funded rival Handy, so when funding failed to materialize the company had no cushion left.
timingNote: Timing mattered: Homejoy hit the worker-classification legal wave right as investors were growing wary of the whole on-demand-labor category, cutting off its ability to raise a bridge round that might have carried it through the lawsuits.

name: Zaarly
tagline: The Kansas City marketplace that spent a decade pivoting before finally grinding to a halt.
proximateCause: Ceased operations in April 2021 after roughly ten years of repeated pivots — from a 'reverse Craigslist' marketplace to virtual storefronts to home services — failed to find a sustainably profitable model.
rootCause: Zaarly launched as a peer-to-peer 'buyer-powered' marketplace, but shut that model down in 2013 after struggling against Craigslist and TaskRabbit for reach, and pivoted repeatedly afterward. Each pivot bought time but never solved the fundamental problem of building enough two-sided liquidity in local home services to beat better-capitalized rivals. After a decade of what CEO Bo Fishback later called 'grinding,' the company finally closed down in April 2021, with its remaining assets sold to Australian competitor Airtasker for $2.6 million.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem — Zaarly had a full decade to find product-market fit and repeatedly failed to reach the scale needed against Craigslist, TaskRabbit, and later Airtasker.

name: Periscope
tagline: Twitter's live-streaming pioneer that got outpaced by the feeds it inspired.
proximateCause: Twitter formally shut Periscope down on March 31, 2021, pulling it from app stores and ending the ability to broadcast.
rootCause: Twitter acquired Periscope in 2015 before it had even launched, and it briefly won an Apple App of the Year award, but Twitter's own native live video and rivals like Instagram Live and TikTok absorbed the audience for casual mobile live-streaming. Twitter said usage had been declining for years while the maintenance cost of running a separate app kept climbing, and it chose to fold any remaining live functionality into the core Twitter app instead of continuing to support a standalone product in what it called an 'unsustainable maintenance-mode state.'
timingNote: This was a platform-trend timing problem: Periscope peaked early in the live-streaming wave, but by 2020 the feature had become table stakes built directly into Instagram, TikTok, and Twitter itself, leaving no reason for a dedicated app to survive.

name: Xobni
tagline: The contacts-and-inbox plugin Yahoo bought, then switched off a year later.
proximateCause: Yahoo shut down Xobni.com and its Smartr product suite on July 2, 2014, about a year after acquiring the company.
rootCause: Xobni built a popular Outlook (and later Gmail) plugin that surfaced contact info and searchable, people-centric email — features email clients like Gmail and Outlook were increasingly building in natively. Yahoo bought Xobni for more than $60 million in mid-2013 mainly for its team and technology rather than to keep running the product, and folded pieces of it into Yahoo Mail (like compose auto-suggest and people-centric search) before discontinuing the standalone apps entirely in its 2014 'summer cleaning' of underperforming products.
timingNote: Largely a platform-dependency problem rather than pure timing: once major email providers absorbed the contact-intelligence features Xobni pioneered, a standalone plugin no longer had a reason to exist independent of its acquirer's roadmap.

name: Incredibowl
tagline: The Boulder pipe-maker whose cult products couldn't keep the lights on.
proximateCause: Incredibowl Industries officially shut down in 2020, ending production of its well-known i420 and m420 pipes.
rootCause: Incredibowl built a devoted following in the cannabis-accessory niche around its patented spinning-bowl pipe design, made in Boulder, Colorado starting in 2009. But as a small hardware manufacturer it never found a way to scale distribution or fend off cheaper mass-market alternatives available on Amazon and through big smoke-shop chains, and original team members drifted to other projects as the business stalled. Without new capital or a broader retail push, production of its core products wound down and the company closed in 2020.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — legal cannabis accessory retail was actually expanding through the 2010s; Incredibowl's failure was a niche-scale and distribution problem rather than a market-timing one.

name: Spring
tagline: The 'shoppable Instagram' that Instagram itself made obsolete.
proximateCause: New owner ShopRunner shuttered the Spring app and website in 2019, less than a year after acquiring it, folding its marketplace features into its own District app instead.
rootCause: Spring launched as a mobile-first marketplace connecting shoppers directly to brands, and Apple even named it one of the best apps of 2014. But Instagram's own rollout of native shopping and product-tagging features gave users a far larger, more familiar place to discover and buy the same fashion brands, steadily draining Spring's relevance. Unable to reach sustainable scale on its own, Spring sold to ShopRunner in October 2018, which shut the standalone app down within a year to consolidate its shopping features elsewhere.
timingNote: This was a platform-timing problem: Spring's core pitch — a shoppable, visual marketplace — got absorbed directly into Instagram's native feature set, undercutting the reason to use a separate app.

name: AllRomance
tagline: The romance e-book pioneer that closed its doors owing its own authors royalties.
proximateCause: All Romance eBooks abruptly announced it would cease all operations effective December 31, 2016, citing a first-ever annual loss and a bleak 2017 forecast.
rootCause: All Romance built a loyal niche audience among independent romance authors and readers starting in 2006, but as Amazon's Kindle store came to dominate e-book retail, All Romance's sales and market share steadily eroded. By the final quarter of 2016 the company was so cash-strapped that it told the roughly 5,000 authors selling through its site they would receive only 10% of their normal royalty rate, and gave customers just four days to download purchases before the site vanished entirely.
timingNote: Not a pure timing failure — the company survived a full decade before Kindle's dominance became terminal, but it never adapted its niche-retailer model as the broader e-book market consolidated around Amazon.

name: EyeEm
tagline: The Berlin photo-sharing pioneer that outlived three owners before finally going dark.
proximateCause: EyeEm shut down permanently on January 13, 2026, after filing for bankruptcy in 2023 and cycling through two acquirers in three years.
rootCause: EyeEm built a large photographer community and a stock-photo marketplace, but never found a monetization model that could compete with giants like Getty Images and the free-stock disruption from Unsplash. It was acquired by Talenthouse for close to $40 million in 2021, filed for bankruptcy in April 2023, and was bought again by Freepik that October — but even under new ownership, and after a controversial 2024 policy change requiring photographers to grant rights for AI-training use of their images, the platform could not rebuild a sustainable business and was shut down for good in January 2026.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem: EyeEm's stock-photography niche was squeezed from both ends — free platforms like Unsplash undercut casual demand, while AI image generation began eating into stock-photo licensing just as the company was trying to recover from bankruptcy.

name: Path
tagline: The private social network that traded trust for growth and never got it back.
proximateCause: Path announced it was shutting down and stopped operating in September 2018, after being acquired by South Korea's Kakao three years earlier failed to revive it.
rootCause: Path built an intimate, close-friends alternative to Facebook and raised over $50 million from top investors, even turning down a reported $100 million acquisition offer from Google in 2011. But a series of privacy scandals broke user trust: in 2012 it was caught uploading users' phone contacts without permission, and in 2013 the FTC fined it $800,000 for illegally collecting data from children under 13, on top of unsolicited SMS spam that got it cut off from Facebook's Find Friends. The reputational damage combined with fierce competition from Instagram and Snapchat for the same close-friends-sharing use case, and after being acquired by Kakao in 2015, Path was quietly shut down in 2018.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem — Path's core failure was self-inflicted privacy scandals during a period when trust was cheap to lose and hard to win back, compounded by Instagram and Snapchat's growth in the same market.

name: GoPro Karma
tagline: GoPro's drone bet that crashed before it could fly straight.
proximateCause: GoPro discontinued the Karma drone entirely on January 9, 2018, alongside cutting more than 20% of its workforce, after disappointing holiday sales.
rootCause: Karma launched in October 2016 into a market DJI already dominated, and stumbled immediately: GoPro had to recall every unit in November 2016 after units lost power and fell out of the sky due to a battery-latch defect. Even after a February 2017 relaunch with a fixed design, the drone never recovered its reputation, and GoPro had to heavily discount unsold inventory — taking an $80 million hit — during the 2017 holiday season. With Q4 2017 revenue landing far below projections, GoPro chose to exit the drone category entirely rather than keep competing with DJI's far more mature product line.
timingNote: This was more an execution failure than a timing one: GoPro entered the consumer drone market at a reasonable moment, but a rushed, defective launch handed the advantage straight to DJI before Karma had a chance to compete on merits.

name: Pearl Automation
tagline: The Apple-veteran hardware startup that couldn't out-build Detroit's own backup cameras.
proximateCause: Pearl Automation shut down in June 2017, roughly three years after founding, after selling off its RearVision product to American Road Products.
rootCause: Pearl Automation, founded by former Apple engineers, built aftermarket backup-camera and safety hardware for cars — a category automakers themselves were rapidly making standard equipment, especially after U.S. regulators mandated rearview cameras in all new cars by 2018. That regulatory tailwind for OEM-built cameras undercut the market for a premium aftermarket add-on, and despite raising $50 million from investors like Accel and Shasta Ventures, Pearl couldn't generate enough sales momentum to justify continuing, folding after selling its core product line.
