timingNote: This was a bad-timing story: Pearl launched premium aftermarket backup cameras right as federal regulation was about to make built-in cameras standard on nearly every new car, closing its market window before the company could scale.

name: Vdio
tagline: Rdio's video side-bet that lasted less than nine months.
proximateCause: Rdio discontinued Vdio on December 27, 2013, less than nine months after launching it that April.
rootCause: Vdio tried to extend Rdio's music-streaming subscriber base into pay-per-view movie and TV rentals, competing directly against iTunes, Amazon Video, and the fast-rising Netflix at a moment when video licensing costs and negotiating leverage overwhelmingly favored incumbents. Rdio itself was under financial pressure (it would file for bankruptcy less than two years later, in 2015) and couldn't sustain a side venture with unproven demand, so it cut Vdio quickly rather than keep investing in a market it wasn't positioned to win.
timingNote: This was a timing and resourcing problem: Rdio launched a capital-intensive video service while its core music business was already struggling to compete with Spotify, leaving no room to give the new bet the multi-year runway video-on-demand typically needs.

name: Theranos
tagline: The blood-testing unicorn whose miracle device never actually worked.
proximateCause: Theranos formally ceased operations in September 2018 after its core blood-testing technology was exposed as fraudulent and its $9 billion valuation evaporated.
rootCause: Theranos claimed its proprietary Edison devices could run comprehensive diagnostic panels from a single finger-prick of blood, but the technology never worked reliably — the company was secretly running most tests on modified third-party machines while presenting the results as its own breakthrough. Investigative reporting by the Wall Street Journal's John Carreyrou beginning in 2015 exposed the deception, triggering SEC, FDA, and CMS investigations that found the company's lab posed 'immediate jeopardy to patient health and safety.' By 2016 Theranos had to void two years of test results, and founder Elizabeth Holmes and president Sunny Balwani were later convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy.
timingNote: Not a timing problem at all — this was a straightforward fraud case in which the core technology simply never worked, regardless of market conditions.

name: Wesabe
tagline: The finance app that lost the category it helped invent to Mint.
proximateCause: Wesabe shut down its service on July 31, 2010, after announcing the closure a month earlier.
rootCause: Wesabe launched in December 2005 as one of the first web tools to automatically analyze users' bank data and offer money-saving advice, and raised $4 million in funding. But rival Mint.com launched a smoother, faster onboarding experience (users didn't have to manually download and upload their bank statements as Wesabe initially required) and out-executed Wesabe in growth and fundraising, eventually getting acquired by Intuit for $170 million in 2009. Wesabe never closed that execution gap, and by mid-2010 it had run out of runway and shut down, releasing an open-source version of its code for users who wanted to run it themselves.
timingNote: This was more an execution-speed problem than a timing one — Wesabe and Mint launched around the same time, but Mint's faster, easier onboarding won the category outright.

name: Airware
tagline: The commercial-drone platform that burned through top-tier VC money chasing a market that wasn't ready.
proximateCause: Airware ceased operations on September 14, 2018, after burning through more than $100 million in venture funding without reaching profitability.
rootCause: Airware set out to build the operating system and analytics platform for commercial and industrial drones, betting that enterprises across construction, mining, and agriculture would need a common software layer the way PCs needed Windows. But DJI came to dominate the hardware side of the market with cheap, capable drones, while enterprise adoption of industrial drone software proved slower and more fragmented than investors like Andreessen Horowitz, Kleiner Perkins, and Intel had bet on. Unable to find a profitable niche fast enough to justify its cash burn, Airware shut down and sold its remaining technology and IP to French drone company Delair.
timingNote: This was a timing problem: Airware raised big money on the assumption that industrial drone software would scale quickly, but enterprise adoption lagged years behind the funding cycle that backed it.

name: Foodler
tagline: The Boston food-delivery pioneer that folded into the rival it once tried to beat.
proximateCause: Foodler's website shut down on October 17, 2017, with all customer orders migrated to GrubHub after GrubHub acquired the company that June.
rootCause: Foodler built one of the earliest online food-ordering aggregators, launching well before national scale players entered the space, but it never achieved the geographic density or delivery infrastructure that GrubHub and, later, DoorDash and Uber Eats built through years of aggressive fundraising and expansion. Facing a market consolidating around a few dominant platforms, Foodler agreed to sell to onetime rival GrubHub in June 2017, which folded Foodler's restaurant network and customers directly into its own platform and retired the Foodler brand entirely within months.
timingNote: This was mostly a scale problem rather than timing — Foodler had a first-mover advantage for over a decade, but consolidation in food delivery ultimately rewarded whichever platform could out-fund and out-expand the others, which wasn't Foodler.

name: ReadyForZero
tagline: The debt-payoff app whose acquirer killed it off within two years.
proximateCause: Avant (which had acquired ReadyForZero in February 2015 under its prior name AvantCredit) shut down ReadyForZero's credit score and debt planner tools on November 12, 2016, deactivating all user accounts.
rootCause: ReadyForZero built a well-regarded tool for tracking and paying down debt, but as a small standalone product it faced the same challenge many personal-finance apps did in competing for attention and trust against Mint and, later, the free credit-monitoring juggernaut Credit Karma. Rather than continuing to invest in a separate consumer brand, Avant acquired ReadyForZero mainly for its team and technology, used the acquisition to open a Los Angeles office, and within about a year and a half decided to fold the product entirely rather than keep running two overlapping consumer-finance tools.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing issue — this was a straightforward post-acquisition product consolidation, where the acquiring company had no strategic reason to keep a redundant tool alive.

name: Pebble
tagline: The Kickstarter smartwatch pioneer that Apple Watch and Fitbit swallowed whole.
proximateCause: Pebble shut down in December 2016 and sold its core software and engineering team to Fitbit for $40 million, discontinuing all hardware production.
rootCause: Pebble popularized the modern smartwatch category with a record-breaking Kickstarter campaign in 2012, years before Apple or Google entered the space. But once Apple Watch launched in 2015 with the ecosystem advantages of iOS integration, App Store support, and Apple's marketing reach, Pebble's simpler, battery-friendly watches lost their edge, and the company couldn't raise the capital needed to keep competing on hardware. Fitbit acquired Pebble's software and patents but explicitly declined to take on its hardware business, and Pebble's existing devices were left to keep working with steadily reduced service quality.
timingNote: This was a timing and ecosystem problem: Pebble won early with a novel product category, but once platform giants like Apple entered with vertically integrated hardware-software-store ecosystems, an independent hardware startup could not keep pace.

name: Refresh
tagline: A social CRM app LinkedIn bought just to shut down two weeks later
proximateCause: LinkedIn acquired Refresh.io in April 2015 and shut down the standalone consumer app almost immediately.
rootCause: Refresh built a 'digital briefing book' app that surfaced social-network insights about people before you met them. LinkedIn wanted the 15-person team and its predictive-insights technology, not the product itself — 12 of 15 employees moved to LinkedIn's own teams in Mountain View while the app was killed. It was a talent acquisition dressed up as a product one.
timingNote: Not a timing problem. Refresh had real traction and technology; it died because its acquirer wanted the team and IP, not the standalone product.

name: Gimlet
tagline: The prestige podcast studio Spotify bought for $230M and dissolved four years later
proximateCause: Spotify cut roughly 200 podcast-division jobs in June 2023 and sunset Gimlet as a standalone studio, folding what remained into Spotify Studios.
rootCause: Spotify acquired Gimlet in 2019 betting that prestige, narrative-driven podcasting would drive subscriptions. But scripted, produced shows like the ones Gimlet made were expensive relative to the ad and subscription revenue they generated. As Spotify pivoted toward cheaper creator- and video-focused podcasting, it cancelled Gimlet's remaining shows and retired the studio brand entirely.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem: Gimlet was bought at the peak of the podcast-studio land grab in 2019, and by 2023 the market had swung hard toward inexpensive creator content, exposing its cost structure.

name: Outdoor Voices
tagline: The activewear darling that closed every store before a distressed sale saved it as a shell
proximateCause: In March 2024, Outdoor Voices closed all 16 of its retail stores and laid off about 80% of its corporate staff amid reports of imminent bankruptcy, before being acquired out of distress two months later.
rootCause: Outdoor Voices expanded into brick-and-mortar retail and new product lines faster than its cash flow could support, racking up unpaid supplier debts (one supplier sued for $2.5M). Facing near-certain Chapter 11, the company was sold to Consortium Brand Partners in May 2024 as an online-only remnant of its former self.
timingNote: Less a timing problem than a cash-management one — activewear demand kept growing industry-wide (Lululemon included); Outdoor Voices specifically overspent on physical footprint its margins couldn't support.

name: Skully Helmets
tagline: The AR motorcycle helmet that ran out of cash while its founders allegedly spent on strippers and sports cars
proximateCause: Skully ran out of money and shut down in August 2016, days after a lawsuit alleged its founders had misused company funds.
rootCause: Skully's own bookkeeper sued founders Marcus and Mitchell Weller, alleging company money paid for two Dodge Vipers, a rented Lamborghini, apartment rent, and strip-club bills, concealed through fraudulent bookkeeping. Of roughly 3,300 helmets sold through Indiegogo and an $11M Series A, only about 200 ever shipped, leaving thousands of backers with nothing when the company folded.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — augmented-reality helmets were a genuinely novel idea with real backer demand; alleged fraud and mismanagement by leadership killed it, not the market.

name: ThredUp Goody Box
tagline: ThredUp's styling-by-mail experiment that lost to its own core marketplace
proximateCause: ThredUp discontinued its Goody Box personal-styling subscription service on October 15, 2021.
rootCause: Goody Box paired a styling fee with a curated box of ten secondhand items, but ThredUp learned its core marketplace shoppers loved the thrill of the hunt themselves, while Goody Box customers wanted more styling guidance than a subscription box could deliver — two incompatible desires under one brand. Rather than keep subsidizing the niche product, ThredUp cut it to refocus on its core marketplace and its Rescue Box successor.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — this was an internal product-market-fit mismatch with ThredUp's own customer base, not an external market shift.

name: Shopkick
tagline: The pioneering shopping-rewards app that survived three owners before vanishing overnight
proximateCause: Shopkick shut down abruptly on March 27, 2026, cutting users off from unredeemed reward balances with no advance warning.
rootCause: Shopkick pioneered location-based shopping rewards in 2009 and was sold to image-recognition firm Trax in 2019. Trax spent years simplifying its portfolio around its core retail-analytics business, selling off other units while insisting it would keep Shopkick — but the consumer rewards app was ultimately the odd one out, and the company cited 'market conditions that make it impossible to continue operating the service' when it pulled the plug.
timingNote: More a strategic-fit problem than a market-timing one — shopper-rewards apps still work for others; Shopkick specifically didn't fit its parent's long-term direction.

name: Quixey
tagline: The app-search engine that burned $130M before Apple and Google built its idea in natively
proximateCause: Quixey shut down in February 2017 after failing to secure new funding and defaulting on a loan from Alibaba.
rootCause: Quixey raised over $130M — including a 2015 round from Alibaba and Eric Schmidt's Innovation Endeavors at a roughly $600M valuation — to build a search engine for finding apps by what they could do rather than their name. It never found durable revenue, missed targets through 2016, burned through leadership changes, and was squeezed out as Apple and Google built native app-discovery directly into their own platforms.
timingNote: Timing mattered a lot — Quixey's core problem (discovering apps) was always one the platform owners would eventually solve themselves, and they did just as Quixey needed to monetize.

name: Mailbox
tagline: The email app so beloved Dropbox bought it, then couldn't figure out what to do with it
proximateCause: Dropbox announced in December 2015 that it would shut down Mailbox, and the app went dark on February 26, 2016.
rootCause: Dropbox acquired the acclaimed swipe-based email app in 2013 for a reported $100M, but Mailbox never became core to Dropbox's business. As Dropbox refocused on collaboration and file-sharing, and as Gmail, Outlook, and others copied Mailbox's swipe-and-snooze gestures, the standalone app lost its differentiation and its reason for existing inside Dropbox.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem — Mailbox's signature UX ideas got absorbed into mainstream email clients within a couple of years, closing the gap that justified keeping a separate app alive.

name: Fab.com
tagline: The flash-sale unicorn that burned $336M chasing 'the Amazon of design'
proximateCause: Fab sold its digital and e-commerce assets to PCH International in March 2015 for a fraction of its once-over-$1B valuation, effectively ending the original company.
rootCause: Fab pivoted from a gay social network into flash-sale design e-commerce and grew explosively on paid-acquisition-driven growth, raising $336M at a peak valuation north of $1B. Its unit economics never worked — customer acquisition costs outpaced lifetime value, a costly European expansion drained cash, and repeated strategic pivots (flash sales, then full-price retail, then a curated marketplace) confused customers and investors alike. When a planned $150M round collapsed, the company laid off most of its staff and sold what remained rather than shut down outright.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem — flash-sale e-commerce worked for contemporaries like Gilt and HauteLook in the same window; Fab's failure was self-inflicted through unsustainable growth spending and strategic whiplash.

name: Aptera Motors
tagline: The three-wheeled 200-mpg concept car that ran out of money before it reached the road
proximateCause: Aptera announced in December 2011 it was ceasing operations and liquidating, auctioning off its prototypes, tooling, and Carlsbad, California facility.
rootCause: Aptera couldn't raise the private matching investment needed to unlock a $150M Department of Energy loan it had been offered, and a proposed acquisition by Next Autoworks fell through. Despite years of prototypes and hype around its ultra-efficient three-wheeled design, it never reached production, and when investor patience ran out the board chose an orderly wind-down over bankruptcy — creditors and depositors were reportedly repaid in full.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem — Aptera was chasing the same DOE loan-program money and investor attention as Tesla and Fisker, and lost that race before EVs had a mass market to sell into. (A separate, unrelated company later revived the Aptera name in 2019.)

name: SamplingLab
tagline: The free-samples storefront that couldn't turn foot traffic into a business
proximateCause: SamplingLab's Portland storefront closed permanently in February 2016.
rootCause: SamplingLab let shoppers walk out with free full-size products in exchange for feedback, drawing real buzz — over 9,000 Portlanders visited and it landed coverage in the Wall Street Journal and Business Insider. But trading free inventory for data isn't a business model that scales on its own, and founder Jeff Davis couldn't convert the attention into a sustainable retail concept.
timingNote: Not really a timing problem — the novelty of 'everything is free' drove interest regardless of market conditions; the issue was monetization, not market readiness.

name: Selltag
tagline: The Spanish social marketplace its own CEO walked away from mid-raise
proximateCause: Selltag shut down in August 2015 after its CEO exited and abandoned an in-progress funding round.
rootCause: The Valencia-based mobile marketplace had racked up 250,000 downloads and 55,000 registered users, but engagement and retention never reached a level the CEO felt justified further investment; mobile marketplaces had become a capital-intensive game requiring critical mass on both sides that Selltag hadn't reached. When the CEO walked away mid-raise, the remaining team and investors tried to keep it alive but ultimately couldn't.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — social commerce was a live category at the time; Selltag's issue was never building enough two-sided liquidity to justify the capital required.

name: Elio Motors
tagline: The $6,800 three-wheeled car that spent over a decade promising and never delivering
proximateCause: Elio Motors repeatedly missed its own production deadlines for more than a decade and eventually went effectively dark — its factory idle, its website down, and no vehicles ever delivered to the tens of thousands of reservation holders.
rootCause: Elio promised an ultra-cheap ($6,800), 84-mpg three-wheeled vehicle and collected reservation deposits from over 60,000 people, but it never solved manufacturing at scale, repeatedly pushed back launch dates, and burned through funding without shipping a single production unit. Though it never formally filed bankruptcy, it became widely reported as defunct in all but name, its Shreveport, Louisiana factory sitting unused with no public updates from company officers.
timingNote: A genuine timing problem compounds an execution one — Elio bet on high gas prices making an ultra-efficient three-wheeler attractive, but by the time it might have shipped, cheap gas and the shift toward EVs had eroded the case for its design entirely.

name: Mobli
tagline: The celebrity-backed Instagram rival that filed for bankruptcy after burning $86M
proximateCause: Mobli shut its Israeli R&D center, laid off its remaining staff, and declared bankruptcy in 2016.
rootCause: Backed by celebrity investors including Leonardo DiCaprio and Serena Williams, Mobli tried to out-feature Instagram with location- and hashtag-based visual search and live video, but never matched Instagram's network effects or found a differentiated enough experience once Instagram and Snapchat added the same features. After layoffs and closure, the remaining team salvaged some value by selling Mobli's geofilters patent to Snapchat for over $7M in 2017.
timingNote: Timing was central — Mobli launched alongside Instagram, but Facebook's 2012 acquisition of Instagram gave its rival essentially unlimited resources and distribution Mobli could never match.

name: Clinkle
tagline: Silicon Valley's most infamous seed round: $25M for a mobile wallet that never really shipped
proximateCause: Clinkle effectively shut down by mid-2016 after investors demanded their money back and the workforce shrank from 70 to about a dozen consultants.
rootCause: Clinkle raised what was then the largest seed round in Silicon Valley history ($25M in 2013) on founder Lucas Duplan's vision for mobile payments, but the app stayed in limited beta with barely any functionality through 2014, cycled through executives (including a five-month stint by former Netflix CFO Barry McCarthy), and saw seven core employees quit in protest in 2015. By the time it had anything resembling a product, Venmo and Apple Pay had already delivered what Clinkle had only promised.
timingNote: Timing was fatal — Clinkle spent years failing to ship while the mobile-payments category it hoped to define got solved by better-resourced, faster-moving competitors.

name: Twitter Fabric
tagline: Twitter's developer platform that Google bought, then killed anyway
proximateCause: Google, which acquired Fabric and its core Crashlytics component from Twitter in January 2017, fully deprecated Fabric on March 31, 2020, forcing remaining developers onto Firebase.
rootCause: Twitter built Fabric out of Crashlytics (which it bought for over $100M in 2013) into a broader mobile developer toolkit covering analytics, crash reporting, and beta distribution, reaching a billion devices within eight months of its 2014 launch. But Fabric was a distraction from Twitter's core ad business; in 2017 Twitter sold it to Google, which folded Crashlytics into Firebase and spent the next three years migrating developers off Fabric before shutting it down for good.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem — Fabric was technically successful and widely adopted; it died because its owner's strategic priorities shifted twice, not because the market moved past it.

name: BranchOut
tagline: The 'LinkedIn on Facebook' app that Facebook's own platform changes starved to death
proximateCause: After raising $49M and growing to 33 million users, BranchOut ran out of runway and was in talks to sell its mobile team and technology to Hearst by September 2014.
rootCause: BranchOut built its entire growth engine on Facebook's viral distribution tools — the same open-graph and notification mechanics that let it recruit tens of millions of users cheaply. When Facebook changed those viral mechanics, and LinkedIn separately cut off BranchOut's API access over a paid enterprise recruiting tool, BranchOut's user acquisition collapsed almost overnight, and it couldn't build a sustainable, platform-independent business before funding ran out.
timingNote: Timing and platform dependency were the whole story — BranchOut's rise and fall tracked Facebook's platform policy changes almost exactly.

name: Topix
tagline: The local-news forum site that outlasted a decade of trolls before quietly closing
proximateCause: Topix shut down its local news and community forums on December 20, 2018.
rootCause: Topix ran anonymous, town-by-town discussion boards for over a decade, but the forums became infamous for unmoderated gossip and harassment (and were even used in criminal investigations), overwhelming the 'news and discussion' identity Topix wanted. In its own shutdown announcement, the company admitted that 'as Topix grew, news and discussion became less of what we are all about,' pivoting instead toward entertainment before being acquired by Publishers Clearing House in 2019.
timingNote: Largely a trend-shift problem — Facebook and other social platforms absorbed the local-gossip function Topix's forums once served, leaving its core product increasingly toxic without an offsetting audience benefit.

name: Driver
tagline: The $90M cancer-trial-matching startup that shut down two months after launch
proximateCause: Driver shut its doors in November 2018, just two months after a high-profile launch, after running out of money.
rootCause: Driver combined molecular pathology labs in the US and China with a consumer app matching cancer patients to clinical trials, backed by roughly $90M from Hong Kong billionaire Li Ka-Shing's Horizon Ventures and partnerships with more than 30 major cancer hospitals. But none of those hospitals actually paid Driver, and the company couldn't close deals with drugmakers or insurers to monetize the matching service — despite elite backing and real technology, it had no viable revenue model and laid off all roughly 85 employees within weeks of running dry.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — cancer-trial matching remains a real unsolved need. Driver's failure was a business-model one: nobody in its network of hospitals, drugmakers, or insurers agreed to actually pay for the service.

name: Monitor110
tagline: The Wall Street sentiment-monitoring startup that launched a decade before its market existed
proximateCause: Monitor110 shut down in July 2008 after failing to close a new funding round.
rootCause: Monitor110 built an algorithm to scan roughly 40 million online sources — blogs, forums, filings — to surface early signals for Wall Street investors, raising more than $20M total from backers including DFJ. The product suffered from spam and duplicate content polluting its results, indecisive leadership delayed a needed pivot, and by the time the company settled on a new direction it had already burned through its funding; a final 2008 financing round fell through and the company closed that July.
timingNote: A real timing problem — Monitor110 was attempting algorithmic social-sentiment analysis for finance nearly a decade before Twitter-based sentiment trading and modern NLP made that approach commercially viable.

name: Yahoo Live
tagline: Yahoo's live-streaming bet that lasted barely a year
proximateCause: Yahoo shut down Yahoo Live at 7:07pm EST on December 3, 2008, little more than a year after launch.
rootCause: Yahoo Live let anyone broadcast a live webcam stream directly on Yahoo's platform, but it never found meaningful adoption against the backdrop of Yahoo's broader struggles and a live-streaming market that wasn't ready — mainstream broadband, mobile cameras, and audience habits for casual live video were all years away from supporting the product Yahoo was offering.
timingNote: A clear timing problem — live streaming for ordinary users didn't go mainstream until platforms like Periscope, Twitch, and Instagram/Facebook Live arrived years later, once mobile bandwidth and camera quality caught up.

name: Yahoo Buzz
tagline: Yahoo's answer to Digg, cut in a round of 'underperforming product' cleanups
proximateCause: Yahoo shut down Yahoo Buzz on April 21, 2011, as part of a broader cut of underperforming products alongside Delicious and AltaVista.
rootCause: Yahoo Buzz, launched in November 2008, let users rate and share news stories in a Digg-style social-news format. It never built the critical mass of engaged curators that made Digg (and later Reddit) work, and as new Yahoo leadership pushed to 'cut investment in underperforming or off-strategy products,' Buzz was an easy target years after its main competitor had already defined the category.
timingNote: A real timing problem — Yahoo Buzz launched three years after Digg had already established social-news curation, entering a category where the first mover's community effects were hard to dislodge.

name: Hitpost
tagline: The scrappy sports-app maker Yahoo bought just to shut down and absorb the team
proximateCause: Yahoo acquired Hitpost in October 2013 and immediately shut down its apps, moving the entire seven-person team into Yahoo Sports.
rootCause: Hitpost built a string of sports-fan apps — including Fantasy Football Polls and a sports-prediction game — trying to carve out a niche in social sports engagement. Rather than scale as an independent company, it became one of Marissa Mayer-era Yahoo's many acqui-hires, where Yahoo valued the small team's talent over the product, discontinuing Hitpost's apps entirely upon acquisition.
timingNote: Not really a timing problem — this was a talent acquisition; Hitpost's products were killed regardless of market fit because Yahoo wanted the team, not the app.

name: Sherpaa
tagline: The virtual-primary-care pioneer whose acquirer wound it down 18 months later
proximateCause: Crossover Health, which acquired Sherpaa's technology platform in February 2019, fully wound Sherpaa down by December 2020 after an announced transition period.
rootCause: Sherpaa, founded by Dr. Jay Parkinson, pioneered asynchronous-messaging-based virtual primary care for self-insured employers years before telehealth went mainstream, but it struggled to land and retain enough large employer clients to reach scale on its own. Crossover Health acquired its technology and most of its staff to fold into its own hybrid physical-and-virtual care platform, absorbing the product's ideas while discontinuing the standalone service.
timingNote: A genuine timing problem — Sherpaa was doing what became 'virtual primary care' nearly a decade before COVID-19 made telehealth mainstream, and it ran out of scale before the market caught up to justify its model independently.

name: Light
tagline: The 16-lens smartphone-camera disruptor that pivoted to cars, then got absorbed and dissolved
proximateCause: Light abandoned consumer cameras for automotive imaging in 2020, and in May 2022 John Deere acquired its remaining assets and hired its staff, after which Light was formally dissolved.
rootCause: Light's L16 camera used 16 small lenses and computational photography to try to match DSLR image quality in a compact body, but by the time it shipped in 2017, smartphone cameras — especially with multi-lens phones and computational photography from Apple and Google — had closed the quality gap Light was built to exploit. After a failed pivot to automotive and robotics imaging, Light ran out of independent runway and was absorbed by John Deere.
timingNote: A clear timing problem — Light spent years building a specialized multi-lens camera just as smartphone makers were about to solve the same computational-photography problem inside a device people already carried.

name: uBiome
tagline: The microbiome-testing unicorn undone by an FBI raid over billing fraud
proximateCause: FBI agents raided uBiome's San Francisco offices in April 2019 investigating insurance billing fraud, and the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy that September before converting to Chapter 7 liquidation in October 2019.
rootCause: uBiome offered at-home microbiome testing kits, but insiders alleged the company repeatedly billed patients' insurance without proper consent and pressured doctors to approve tests regardless of medical necessity, part of a scheme prosecutors say defrauded investors and insurers of roughly $60 million. Cofounders Jessica Richman and Zachary Apte were later criminally charged and became SEC-named fugitives after relocating to Germany; they had also reportedly misrepresented their ages to qualify for '30 under 30'-style recognition, part of a broader pattern of misrepresentation the company was built on.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — this was an execution and ethics failure. The underlying microbiome-testing market kept growing via competitors; uBiome specifically died because of fraud.

name: Imercive
tagline: A pivot half-finished, and out of seed money to finish it.
proximateCause: The company ran out of its seed funding before it could execute a pivot away from its original, unworkable business model.
rootCause: Imercive, founded by Keith Nowak, originally aimed to let people order from local restaurants via instant messages, but that concept turned out to be too difficult and expensive to make functional. Nowak tried to pivot to a broader vision of using instant messaging to interact with all kinds of businesses, but by the time he recognized the bigger opportunity, the company had already burned through most of its seed round with no results to show funders. As Nowak put it in his post-mortem, the company was 'caught mid-pivot' between a strategy it knew wouldn't work and one it believed could succeed but couldn't pursue aggressively enough.
timingNote: Not really a timing problem in the market sense - it was a runway problem. The company recognized a better opportunity too late relative to its cash reserves, not too late relative to the market.

name: Chef'd
tagline: Ran out of runway one funding round short of the finish line.
proximateCause: Chef'd abruptly shut down and suspended all operations in July 2018 after failing to raise additional funding to keep going.
rootCause: Despite raising more than $40M in venture funding and partnering with retailers, Chef'd operated a capital-intensive meal-kit business at a time when giants like Blue Apron and HelloFresh were burning cash to buy market share. When a funding round fell through, CEO Kyle Ransford told employees there were 'unexpected circumstances with the funding for the business,' and the company laid off more than 350 workers and closed its Brooklyn and California warehouses essentially overnight.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem: Chef'd entered the meal-kit wars during a period of massive over-investment across the category, competing for the same investor dollars as much better-funded rivals just as enthusiasm for the sector was cooling.

name: MoveLoot
tagline: The logistics of moving other people's couches ate the company.
proximateCause: Move Loot shut down its marketplace operations and sold its customer list to home-services startup Handy rather than continue operating.
rootCause: Move Loot built a full-service curated marketplace for secondhand furniture, handling pickup, storage, and delivery logistics itself, which made every transaction expensive to fulfill. After raising $22M and expanding quickly across multiple US cities following its 2013 launch, the company couldn't keep service quality consistent, with customers complaining about listings not being accepted and goods not being delivered, and it ultimately couldn't make the logistics-heavy model profitable.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing issue - the used-furniture logistics problem it hit is structural, the same one that has sunk similar marketplaces both before and since.

name: Readability
tagline: Tried to pay writers and got squeezed from both sides for it.
proximateCause: Readability shut down its bookmarking and read-later service on September 30, 2016, after failing to find a buyer.
rootCause: Readability tried an idealistic revenue model that shared 70% of subscriber fees with the publishers and writers whose content people saved to read later, but the model pleased almost no one: publishers resented a middleman charging on top of their content, and Apple's in-app purchase cut took another 30% off the top. Meanwhile free competitor Pocket dropped its own paid tier, went fully free on venture funding, and got built directly into Firefox, starving Readability of the audience it needed to sustain a paid model.
timingNote: More a business-model problem than a timing one - Readability entered a market where a well-funded free competitor could simply out-wait a paid one.

name: Grubwithus
tagline: Getting strangers to a shared table was harder to scale than it looked.
proximateCause: GrubWithUs shut down its social dining platform in March 2015 after a pivot to a location-based app called Superb also failed to gain traction.
rootCause: GrubWithUs organized group dinners among strangers with shared interests, but as CEO Eddy Lu later explained, 'too many variables had to align perfectly for it to work' - matching the right people, restaurant, time, and price point at scale proved too operationally heavy. The company had already cut its on-demand GrubTonight product and pivoted the core team to a new app, Superb, before shutting down entirely when neither found a sustainable audience.
timingNote: Not fundamentally a timing problem - the coordination friction in group dining among strangers is structural, and later social-dining and events startups have run into the same wall.

name: Quirky
tagline: A crowd that voted on ideas wasn't the crowd that bought products.
proximateCause: Quirky filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2015 after running out of cash.
rootCause: Quirky's model of crowdsourcing, vetting, and manufacturing new consumer product ideas from a community of a million registered inventors proved too expensive relative to sales. Its own community-voting system for picking which ideas to manufacture wasn't actually predicting which products customers would buy, so weak sales repeatedly failed to cover high development and manufacturing costs. When cash ran critically low in mid-2015, Quirky slashed inventor royalties from 10% down to as little as 1.5%, alienating the community its whole model depended on, and CEO Ben Kaufman stepped down shortly before the bankruptcy filing.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem - the mismatch between what an anonymous voting crowd finds interesting and what paying retail customers actually buy is a structural flaw in the crowdsourced-invention model.

name: Tradesy
tagline: A US resale pioneer absorbed into its bigger European rival.
proximateCause: Tradesy was acquired by Paris-based Vestiaire Collective in March 2022, and its standalone app and website were shut down and redirected into the Vestiaire Collective platform.
rootCause: Tradesy built one of the first dedicated marketplaces for authenticated designer resale in the US, but scaling authentication, trust, and inventory operations against well-capitalized global rivals proved costly. As the resale category consolidated, Europe's much larger Vestiaire Collective bought Tradesy to gain a US foothold, moved its 7 million members onto the Vestiaire platform, and wound the Tradesy brand down entirely rather than run it as a separate business.
timingNote: More a scale problem than a timing one - resale marketplaces were consolidating globally, and Tradesy ended up as the acquired party rather than the consolidator.

name: Markafoni
tagline: A Turkish flash-sale giant that its own parent decided to close.
proximateCause: South African media conglomerate Naspers, which owned 100% of Markafoni, shut the site down effective June 30, 2017.
rootCause: Markafoni grew quickly on a flash-sale model, expanding into Australia, Greece, Poland, and Ukraine after Naspers first took a majority stake in 2011 and then full ownership by 2014. But the flash-sale category faced intensifying local competition and a difficult Turkish economic environment, and the business wasn't scaling toward sustainability, so its parent company simply decided to close it rather than keep funding it.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem - Markafoni had years of runway and corporate backing; it was a sustained profitability problem that its owner eventually stopped underwriting.

name: Essential Products
tagline: Android's co-creator couldn't out-build Apple and Samsung.
proximateCause: Essential Products shut down entirely on February 12, 2020, after concluding it had 'no clear path' to deliver its next device to customers.
rootCause: Founded by Android co-creator Andy Rubin, Essential launched the Essential Phone in 2017 to critical interest but weak sales against Apple and Samsung's marketing and distribution scale. It canceled its next flagship in 2018 and quietly sought a buyer, then pivoted toward an ambitious voice-first device called Project GEM, unveiled in October 2019. But the company couldn't find a viable path to actually ship and sell it, and shut down rather than keep burning capital chasing a market Apple and Samsung already owned.
timingNote: Not a timing problem - Essential entered the premium smartphone market with real engineering credibility, but hardware distribution and brand loyalty in that category are moats that take years and marketing budgets Essential never had.

name: Cake Financial
tagline: A social network for stock portfolios that Mint out-executed.
proximateCause: Cake Financial discontinued operations on January 14, 2010, when it was acquired by E*Trade.
rootCause: Cake Financial let individual investors track and publicly share their stock portfolio performance, a social-finance niche that never reached the scale of broader personal-finance tools like Mint, which was solving a bigger everyday problem for far more users. Unable to grow beyond a niche audience of portfolio-sharing enthusiasts, the small team sold the technology and shut the consumer product down rather than continue operating it independently.
timingNote: Not really a timing problem - Cake launched into a reasonable early wave of personal-finance web apps; it was a niche-versus-mass-market problem, since it never broadened past portfolio-sharing the way Mint broadened past budgeting.

name: Presto
tagline: Went public via SPAC, then its stock collapsed to a fraction of a cent.
proximateCause: Presto Automation's business and assets were sold off at auction on December 3, 2024 to a consortium led by Remus Capital, after its stock collapsed to essentially zero.
rootCause: Presto (formerly e la Carte) built AI-driven tabletop ordering tablets and later drive-thru voice AI for restaurant chains, and went public via SPAC merger in 2022 chasing that pivot. But the company burned through cash faster than it could sign and retain restaurant customers, and its stock crashed until shares traded at $0.0001 with a market cap of a few hundred dollars. Rather than survive as a public company, its operating assets were auctioned off and relaunched under a new entity, Presto Phoenix, Inc.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem - Presto rushed a SPAC-funded pivot into drive-thru voice AI just as public-market patience for unprofitable, cash-burning tech listings was evaporating, leaving it with no runway to prove the pivot out.

name: Netscape
tagline: Won the first browser war, then AOL let it fade for a decade.
proximateCause: AOL discontinued the Netscape browser entirely on March 1, 2008, ending support and development for good.
rootCause: Netscape Navigator was the web's first mass-market browser, but Microsoft bundled Internet Explorer free with Windows and out-distributed it during the late-1990s browser wars, and by November 2007 Netscape held just 0.6% market share against Internet Explorer's 77.4%. AOL, which had acquired Netscape in 1999, let development stagnate for years - security researchers called it a liability for going largely unpatched through 2005-2007 - before finally pulling the plug and pointing remaining users to Firefox.
timingNote: This was a timing problem in the sense that Netscape peaked before browsers were bundled with operating systems became the norm - once Microsoft made that move, Netscape's early lead couldn't survive Windows' distribution advantage.

name: Rethink Robotics
tagline: Built friendly factory robots that couldn't out-earn their price tag.
proximateCause: Rethink Robotics ceased operations in October 2018 after failing to find a buyer for the whole company.
rootCause: Rethink built Baxter and Sawyer, collaborative robots designed to work safely alongside humans on factory floors, but cheaper and more precise rivals like Universal Robots and Fanuc out-competed it on cost and return-on-investment for manufacturers. After burning through $150M without reaching profitability, the company shut down; Germany's HAHN Group acquired its patents, trademarks, and Intera 5 software platform, while China's Hunan CoThink Robotics bought roughly 100 Baxter units and North American sales rights.
timingNote: Partly a timing problem - Rethink pioneered collaborative robotics years before the ROI case was proven for most manufacturers, giving lower-cost fast-followers time to catch up on capability while undercutting it on price.

name: Soundwave
tagline: Spotify bought the team and let the standalone app fade.
proximateCause: Spotify acquired Soundwave in January 2016, and the standalone social-music-tracking app was discontinued as its team and technology were absorbed into Spotify.
rootCause: Soundwave, backed by Mark Cuban, let users track and share what they were listening to across services like Spotify and YouTube, essentially building a social layer on top of platforms that could - and eventually did - build that layer themselves. Once Spotify acquired the team specifically to build out its own messaging and social features, there was no reason to keep running Soundwave as an independent product.
timingNote: A timing problem in the sense that a feature-layer startup sitting on top of a platform is only as durable as that platform's willingness to leave the feature unbuilt - Spotify eventually decided to build it in-house.

name: Mozido
tagline: A $185M mobile payments bet undone by its own founder.
proximateCause: Mozido collapsed into defunct status after founder Michael Liberty was charged by the SEC in April 2018 with defrauding investors.
rootCause: Mozido raised a massive $185M to build a mobile payments and wallet platform, bringing in a former HP executive as CEO in 2015 to professionalize the business as it competed against faster-executing rivals like Square. But the company never found the distribution or execution needed to catch up, and its unraveling accelerated when the SEC accused founder Michael Liberty of defrauding investors, a scandal that made the company effectively unfundable and unsellable afterward.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem - Mozido had capital and years to execute against Square; the fatal blow was a governance and fraud problem at the top, not being early or late to mobile payments.

name: Chirp
tagline: A UK startup that turned sound into a data protocol, pivoted to B2B licensing, then was quietly absorbed by Sonos.
description: App to share data via sound
proximateCause: Sonos acquired Chirp outright in February 2020 and pulled its public SDK from availability by March 2020, ending it as an independent company.
rootCause: Chirp's original consumer app for sending data via audio tones never found an everyday problem people actually needed solved, so the company pivoted from a public app to licensing its data-over-sound SDK to other businesses for use cases like transit ticketing and connected toys. That B2B pivot kept Chirp alive for years but never turned it into a self-sustaining business, and it eventually sold itself to Sonos, which folded the technology in and shut down public access to the SDK.
timingNote: Less a timing problem than a product-market-fit one: audio data transfer was a clever technical trick, but QR codes, NFC, and Bluetooth already solved the same handoff problems more reliably by the time Chirp needed mainstream adoption.

name: Hulu Japan
tagline: Hulu's Japanese outpost couldn't out-license local broadcasters and was sold off within three years.
proximateCause: Hulu sold its entire Japan operation, brand, and subscriber base to Nippon Television in February 2014.
rootCause: Hulu launched in Japan in 2011 betting its US-built platform and content relationships would transfer, but it struggled to secure enough locally relevant content and subscribers to justify continued investment from its US parent. Nippon TV, a domestic broadcaster with the local content relationships Hulu lacked, bought the operation and kept the Hulu brand running under its own ownership.
timingNote: A timing and localization problem more than a pure market one: Hulu entered Japan before it had the licensing footprint to compete with domestic broadcasters, and exited even before Netflix arrived in the market.

name: SpoonRocket
tagline: On-demand meals made money on each order but couldn't raise the cash to survive the funding chill.
proximateCause: SpoonRocket told investors in March 2016 it was shutting down its US on-demand meal delivery service after failing to raise a follow-on round.
rootCause: SpoonRocket had actually reached positive contribution margin, selling meals for more than it cost to cook, package, and deliver them, but that wasn't enough to cover overhead in a food-delivery market crowded with deep-pocketed rivals. A prospective acquisition by a quick-service restaurant chain fell through at the last minute, and with the on-demand funding market turning cold in early 2016, the company ran out of runway and shut down in the US (its assets and brand were later picked up by Brazil's iFood).
timingNote: Timing mattered: SpoonRocket died right as investor enthusiasm for subsidized on-demand delivery startups collapsed in early 2016, taking down a wave of similar companies alongside it.

name: Quanergy
tagline: A SPAC-era LiDAR darling went bankrupt less than a year after going public.
proximateCause: Quanergy filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2022 and completed a court-supervised sale of its assets in February 2023.
rootCause: Quanergy went public via a SPAC merger in early 2022 at an implied $1.4 billion valuation, but autonomous-vehicle and industrial LiDAR demand never materialized at the scale investors had priced in, while rivals like Velodyne and Luminar fought over the same shrinking pool of customers and delayed programs. Burning cash with no clear path to profitability, the company ran out of money within a year of its public debut and had to liquidate through Chapter 11.
timingNote: A timing problem: Quanergy went public right as the autonomous-vehicle hype cycle cooled and SPAC-funded hardware companies fell out of favor with investors, leaving it no room to wait out slower-than-expected LiDAR adoption.

name: Jetpac
tagline: An AI travel-guide app built on Instagram photo analysis got acqui-hired and killed within weeks.
proximateCause: Google acquired Jetpac in August 2014 for its image-recognition technology and pulled the company's apps from the App Store within weeks.
rootCause: Jetpac built City Guides, an app that used machine learning to scan public Instagram photos and infer things like a neighborhood's nightlife or scenic quality, but the underlying image-recognition technology was worth far more to Google as a component for its own products than Jetpac's consumer app was worth as a standalone business. Unable to reach independent scale, the small team sold to Google, which absorbed the technology and shut the apps down almost immediately.
timingNote: Not really a timing problem: computer-vision talent was in high demand in 2014, which is exactly why Google wanted the acquisition, but that same scarcity meant Jetpac's product itself was never going to outcompete platform-scale players on its own.

name: Poshmark UK
tagline: Poshmark's UK fashion-resale marketplace lasted about six months before headquarters pulled the plug.
proximateCause: Poshmark abruptly shut down its UK marketplace in November 2023, giving sellers only about a week's notice, just months after formally launching there in May 2023.
rootCause: Poshmark expanded into the UK, Australia, and India to chase international growth, but all three markets stayed small: the combined active user base across the three countries was under 500,000 in the final month, far short of what was needed to justify local operations, marketing, and support. Facing pressure to focus resources, Poshmark's leadership decided to retreat entirely to its core North American business rather than keep subsidizing an underperforming UK launch.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing problem: the UK resale market itself was healthy (Depop and Vinted were both thriving there), but Poshmark launched without the brand recognition or local seller base to compete and pulled out before it could build either.

name: Quibb
tagline: An invite-only professional news-sharing network never grew past a niche, loyal core.
proximateCause: Founder Sandi MacPherson announced in September 2017 that Quibb was shutting down after years of trying to grow the invite-only news-sharing platform.
rootCause: Quibb let professionals share and discuss industry news in a curated, invite-only feed, and it built a genuinely loyal following, but the loyal core never expanded into a mass audience. With only around 12,000 users and a single $650K seed round to work with years after founding, the product stayed a niche tool for a small group of power users rather than the broad professional network it needed to be to sustain a venture-scale business.
timingNote: Less a timing issue than a scale ceiling: Quibb launched into a market LinkedIn already dominated for professional networking, and its curated, invite-only model that made it appealing to early users was the same thing that kept it from ever growing large.

name: Houseparty
tagline: The pandemic's breakout group-video app couldn't hold its audience once Zoom scaled up.
proximateCause: Epic Games, which had acquired Houseparty in 2019, announced in September 2021 that it was shutting the app down entirely the following month.
rootCause: Houseparty rode a massive usage spike during 2020 lockdowns as people sought casual group video hangouts, but that surge proved to be a temporary pandemic peak rather than durable habit formation. As in-person life resumed and Zoom, FaceTime, and Discord absorbed the same use cases with more robust products, Houseparty's engagement collapsed, and Epic decided to fold the team into building social features for its broader metaverse ambitions instead of continuing to run a standalone app.
timingNote: A clear timing story: Houseparty's growth was almost entirely a byproduct of pandemic lockdowns, and once that unusual demand condition ended, the app had no independent reason for people to keep opening it.

name: Burstly
tagline: Apple bought Burstly for its beta-testing tool and killed the ad business within 90 days.
proximateCause: Apple acquired Burstly in February 2014 and gave its SkyRocket mobile ad network customers 90 days' notice before terminating the service.
rootCause: Burstly ran two products: TestFlight, a popular iOS beta-testing platform, and SkyRocket, a mobile ad-mediation and monetization platform. Apple wanted TestFlight to build into its own developer tools, not the advertising business, so after the acquisition it shut down SkyRocket's publishing and SDK agreements within 90 days, effectively ending Burstly's ad platform even as parts of its technology lived on inside Apple's own products.
timingNote: Not a market-timing failure so much as a strategic mismatch: Burstly built a real, working ad business, but its most valuable asset to an acquirer turned out to be the adjacent testing tool, and the ad platform itself was disposable once ownership changed hands.

name: Knewton
tagline: A decade and $180M of adaptive-learning hype ended in a fire-sale to Wiley.
proximateCause: Wiley acquired Knewton's assets in May 2019 for less than $17 million, a fraction of the over $180 million Knewton had raised.
rootCause: Knewton spent years positioning adaptive learning technology as a breakthrough for personalized education, with Pearson as its marquee publishing partner. Pearson ended that partnership in 2017 to build its own competing technology, and other publishers had little incentive to follow where Pearson had led. Facing a high burn rate, no profitable path, and reduced options after losing its anchor partner, Knewton was forced into an asset sale that industry observers openly called a fire sale.
timingNote: Less a timing problem than an overpromising one: adaptive learning's premise was ahead of what the technology and content partnerships of the era could actually deliver, and by the time results underwhelmed, Knewton had already burned through most of its capital.

name: Yahoo Answers
tagline: A once-dominant Q&A community drowned in spam and low-quality content long before Yahoo finally pulled the plug.
proximateCause: Yahoo Answers went read-only on April 20, 2021 and fully ceased operations on May 4, 2021, redirecting users to a Yahoo help page.
rootCause: Yahoo Answers was one of the first mass Q&A platforms, but its open, largely unmoderated format let low-quality answers, spam, and joke responses proliferate over 15+ years, steadily eroding trust in the platform's content. Quora built a competing product around real-name identity and quality-focused moderation, drawing away the users and experts Yahoo Answers needed to stay credible, and Yahoo eventually decided the declining product wasn't worth maintaining as it narrowed its portfolio.
timingNote: More a quality-erosion problem than a timing one: Yahoo Answers had a long, slow decline over more than a decade rather than a sudden market shift, as unmoderated content quality gradually pushed serious users toward better-curated alternatives.

name: Yahoo Groups
tagline: A pioneering online-community platform was left to wither for years before Yahoo finally shut it down.
proximateCause: Yahoo announced in October 2020 that it would shut down Yahoo Groups, and the service went offline in mid-December 2020.
rootCause: Yahoo Groups was an early and once-massive hub for email-list-based communities, but Yahoo stopped meaningfully investing in the product for years as social networks and dedicated community platforms like Facebook Groups and Discord took over the same use cases. With user numbers dwindling and no strategic priority inside Yahoo's shrinking portfolio, the company eventually decided to retire the legacy service rather than keep maintaining it.
timingNote: A neglect story more than a timing one: Yahoo Groups didn't lose to a single better competitor at one moment, it was slowly abandoned by its own owner over more than a decade while alternatives matured around it.

name: Tilt
tagline: A billion-dollar-valued group-payments app was sold to Airbnb and its product was retired.
proximateCause: Airbnb acquired Tilt in February 2017, absorbing its team while winding the standalone group-payments product down.
rootCause: Tilt built a group-payments and crowdfunding app aimed at younger users splitting costs and pooling money for group purchases, and it grew fast enough to reach a reported $400 million valuation. But it never found a durable, defensible business model beyond peer-to-peer collections that companies like GoFundMe and Venmo were also chasing, and growth stalled well short of its valuation. Facing a shrinking set of options, Tilt sold itself to Airbnb, which wanted the team's payments expertise rather than the consumer product itself.
timingNote: More a business-model problem than a timing one: group payments was a real and growing category, but Tilt's specific product never differentiated enough from free alternatives to justify its venture-scale valuation.

name: Babylon Health
tagline: A SPAC-fueled AI telehealth unicorn collapsed into bankruptcy within two years of going public.
proximateCause: Babylon Health's US operations filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy liquidation on August 15, 2023, and its UK business entered administration the following month, with assets sold off for a fraction of its prior valuation.
rootCause: Babylon built a global AI-powered telemedicine business and went public via SPAC merger in October 2021, but it expanded aggressively into markets like the US and Rwanda while its NHS-dependent UK business faced unsustainable economics and years of controversy over unsubstantiated claims about its AI diagnostic tool's accuracy. The combination of overexpansion, data-breach and regulatory disputes, and mounting losses left it unable to raise further capital, and founder Ali Parsa himself later called the SPAC listing an 'unmitigated disaster.'
timingNote: Partly a timing problem: Babylon rode the pandemic-era telehealth boom to a public listing right as investor enthusiasm for unprofitable healthtech SPACs was cresting, then had no cushion once that funding environment reversed sharply in 2022-2023.

name: Vittana
tagline: A Kiva-style microloan nonprofit for student loans in developing countries couldn't scale beyond a niche.
proximateCause: Vittana announced it was shutting down in August 2014, ending its peer-to-peer student microloan platform.
rootCause: Vittana applied Kiva's crowdfunded microloan model specifically to student loans in developing countries, partnering with local microfinance institutions to disburse and collect payments. The model required deep, reliable local lending infrastructure in each country it operated in, and scaling that infrastructure across multiple developing markets proved far harder and slower than growing a donor base, leaving the nonprofit unable to reach the scale needed to sustain itself.
timingNote: Less a timing issue than an operational-scale ceiling: the underlying need for student financing in developing countries was real and durable, but Vittana's model needed years of local infrastructure-building per market that its funding runway couldn't support.

name: WhoSay
tagline: A celebrity-run social platform ended up as a feature inside a big ad agency's toolkit instead of a business of its own.
proximateCause: Viacom acquired WhoSay in January 2018 and folded it into its advertising division, ending its run as an independent platform.
rootCause: WhoSay let celebrities post verified, official content and connect directly with fans and brands, positioning itself as a trusted middleman for celebrity-brand marketing deals. As Twitter, Instagram, and later X matured into the default channels celebrities used to reach audiences and cut deals directly with brands, the need for a separate verified platform run by a third party eroded, and WhoSay's business model narrowed until it made more sense as an internal capability for Viacom's ad business than as its own product.
timingNote: A timing and platform-shift story: WhoSay launched when social platforms hadn't yet built out celebrity verification and brand-partnership tools themselves, and it lost its reason to exist once Instagram and Twitter absorbed those functions natively.

name: Medium One
tagline: An IoT data platform that got swallowed by the cloud giants before it could break out
proximateCause: The company was quietly acqui-hired by IoT platform Breadware in 2022 rather than reaching independent scale.
rootCause: Medium One built a hosted IoT data intelligence platform for smart applications, but customers increasingly defaulted to AWS IoT and other hyperscaler platforms that bundled the same data processing directly into infrastructure they already used. With only about $3M raised, Medium One never had the resources to out-market or out-feature the cloud giants, and it was eventually absorbed into Breadware, ending its run as an independent company.
timingNote: More a platform-dependency and scale problem than a timing problem — Medium One entered IoT data tooling early (2014), but AWS and Google simply built the same capability into infrastructure customers already used.

name: Music.ly
tagline: The lip-sync app that won the audience war but lost its own name to the app it fed
proximateCause: ByteDance shut down the Musical.ly app on August 2, 2018, merging all its users and content directly into TikTok.
rootCause: Musical.ly built a huge global audience (100M+ users) around short lip-sync videos, which caught ByteDance's eye; ByteDance bought it for over $800M in November 2017 specifically to fuse it with the newly launched TikTok. Rather than run two overlapping short-video apps, ByteDance folded Musical.ly's entire user base and content library into TikTok in mid-2018 and retired the Musical.ly brand entirely.
timingNote: Not a timing failure — Musical.ly's product-market fit was strong; it was killed by strategic consolidation after a lucrative acquisition, not by the market moving past it.

name: Pocket
tagline: The read-it-later pioneer that outlived its acquirer's interest by eight years
proximateCause: Mozilla announced in May 2025 that it was shutting Pocket down for good, with the app going offline on July 8, 2025 and saved data deleted by November 2025.
rootCause: Mozilla acquired Pocket in 2017 as its first-ever acquisition, hoping to make save-for-later reading a core part of the Firefox experience. But reading habits shifted toward algorithmic feeds and native save features built directly into Instagram, X, and other platforms, eroding Pocket's standalone value. Mozilla ultimately decided the product no longer fit its focus and wound it down, refunding Premium subscribers.
timingNote: A slow-motion timing failure — Pocket predated the read-it-later category by years, but by 2025 the entire category had been absorbed into native platform features, leaving a standalone app with shrinking reason to exist.

name: Songza
tagline: A mood-based playlist app absorbed into the product it was bought to build
proximateCause: Google shut down the Songza app and website on January 31, 2016, folding its features into Google Play Music.
rootCause: Google acquired Songza in July 2014 specifically for its Concierge mood- and activity-based playlist technology and hand-curated playlists. Over the next year and a half, Google rebuilt those features directly into Google Play Music, and once feature parity was reached, running two nearly identical products no longer made sense, so Songza was retired and its founders moved to the Play Music team.
timingNote: Not a timing failure — Songza succeeded on its own terms and was bought specifically to be merged, which is different from being out-competed.

name: Exec
tagline: An on-demand errand app that cut services down to cleaning, then sold even that
proximateCause: Exec shut down its original on-demand errand service in September 2013 to focus solely on home cleaning, then sold the remaining cleaning business to Handy in January 2014.
rootCause: Founded by Justin Kan, Daniel Kan, and Amir Ghazvinian, Exec tried to build a broad on-demand personal-assistant marketplace covering errands, delivery, furniture assembly, and research, but found the margins on general errands too thin to sustain against better-funded rivals like TaskRabbit. It narrowed to cleaning as its one profitable vertical, then folded that business into Handy rather than continue independently.
timingNote: More a margin and focus problem than a timing problem — on-demand labor marketplaces were very much in vogue in 2012-2014, but Exec spread itself across too many service categories before finding one it could defend.

name: Din
tagline: A curated online grocery platform that couldn't out-hustle Instacart in a crowded field
proximateCause: Din shut down in October 2016 after failing to break out of an increasingly crowded online grocery and meal-ingredient market.
rootCause: Din let customers order the exact ingredients used in dishes from local restaurants and chefs, delivered to their door, but the model required deep local restaurant partnerships that were expensive to build and did not scale beyond a handful of markets. Instacart's much broader grocery selection and greater capital reserves made Din's narrower, curated approach hard to defend, and the company closed after running through its funding.
timingNote: More a market-fit problem than a timing problem — the online grocery wave was well underway by 2013-2016, but Din's local, curated model couldn't scale the way Instacart's broad marketplace could.

name: Fisker Automotive
tagline: A luxury hybrid-electric car company undone by the one battery supplier it bet everything on
proximateCause: Fisker Automotive filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in November 2013 after its sole battery supplier, A123 Systems, went bankrupt and halted production of its Karma sedan.
rootCause: Fisker built its entire production line around A123 Systems as its exclusive lithium-ion battery supplier; when A123 recalled defective battery packs and then filed for bankruptcy in October 2012, Fisker had no backup supplier and was forced to halt production entirely. Combined with a costly national recall and default on a $528M Department of Energy loan, the company burned through its $1.4B in funding and was ultimately sold for parts to Chinese auto-parts maker Wanxiang in 2014.
timingNote: More an execution and supply-chain risk failure than a timing failure — the luxury EV/hybrid category was viable, as Tesla proved in the same window, but Fisker's single-supplier dependency and quality issues sank it before it could scale.

name: Zume
tagline: The robot pizza company that couldn't keep the cheese from sliding off the pie
proximateCause: Zume shut down and liquidated its assets in June 2023 after burning through $445M in venture funding, including $375M from SoftBank.
rootCause: Zume's original pitch was pizzas assembled and cooked by robots inside moving delivery vans, but the company could never solve basic physics problems like cheese sliding off pies during transit, and the hardware proved unreliable at scale. It pivoted away from robotics into compostable packaging in 2020, but that business also failed to find a profitable niche, and Zume chose to liquidate rather than raise again or file for bankruptcy.
timingNote: Not a timing problem — food-delivery robotics and automation were (and remain) a hyped category — this was a hardware execution and unit-economics failure that better timing could not have fixed.

name: Friendster
tagline: The social network that invented the category and then watched Facebook take it
proximateCause: Friendster's remaining social-gaming service went dark on June 14, 2015, ending the site for good after years of decline.
rootCause: Friendster pioneered mainstream social networking in 2002 but was crippled by chronic slow-loading pages and technical scaling failures just as MySpace and then Facebook offered faster, more reliable experiences. After losing its Western user base, Friendster pivoted to a Southeast Asia-focused social gaming platform in 2011, wiping all prior user data, but the gaming pivot never regained meaningful engagement and the company quietly shut down in 2015.
timingNote: A genuine timing failure — Friendster had first-mover advantage in social networking but its infrastructure couldn't keep pace with its own growth, letting Facebook out-execute it during the critical early-adoption window.

name: Yik Yak
tagline: The anonymous campus app that couldn't outrun what its own anonymity enabled
proximateCause: Yik Yak shut down in April 2017 after Square acqui-hired its engineering team for roughly $1M, a steep fall from its earlier $400M valuation.
rootCause: Yik Yak's anonymous, location-based "yaks" made it wildly popular on college campuses, but that same anonymity made it a magnet for cyberbullying, racist threats, and harassment, prompting many schools to ban or block it. User growth collapsed under the reputational damage and a wave of copycat features from Facebook, Twitter, and Snapchat, leaving the company unable to raise further funding before its team was quietly absorbed by Square.
timingNote: Partly a trend problem — anonymous social apps fell out of favor industry-wide as platforms cracked down on abuse — but toxicity and moderation failures were the core cause, not just timing. (The brand was later relaunched in 2021 and acquired by Sidechat in 2023, but the original company never recovered from its 2017 collapse.)

name: Sprig
tagline: A premium meal-delivery startup that offered free delivery until the delivery itself killed the margins
proximateCause: Sprig ceased operations in 2017 after running out of cash trying to sustain a delivery-only, cook-and-deliver model.
rootCause: Sprig prepared and delivered its own organic meals rather than partnering with restaurants, which meant it absorbed the full cost of sourcing, cooking, and courier logistics itself. To stay competitive it offered free delivery, which thinned already-slim margins further, and it could not out-scale better-funded, broader competitors like Uber Eats, Seamless, and Blue Apron who didn't carry the same kitchen overhead.
timingNote: More a unit-economics problem than a timing problem — the meal-delivery boom was in full swing when Sprig operated, but its vertically-integrated cook-and-deliver model was structurally more expensive than marketplace-style competitors.

name: Dinner Lab
tagline: A pop-up fine-dining membership that couldn't deliver enough dinners to keep members paying
proximateCause: Dinner Lab shut down in 2016 after five years of operation once it could no longer sustain its membership-dinner model financially.
rootCause: Dinner Lab charged members a subscription for access to pop-up fine-dining events in unconventional venues, but coordinating food quality, one-off locations, staffing, and registrations for every single event proved operationally brutal and expensive. Members who expected regular dinners sometimes got only one gathering every six weeks, undermining the subscription's value, and an attempt to pivot toward monetizing diner-feedback data for restaurants never made up the shortfall.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing failure — pop-up and experiential dining were culturally on-trend throughout Dinner Lab's run — this was an operational-complexity and unit-economics failure specific to running one-off events at scale.

name: Yo
tagline: The one-word messaging app that proved a viral joke isn't a business
proximateCause: The Yo company itself shut down in 2016, just two years after its April Fools'-Day launch, leaving the app running on autopilot.
rootCause: Yo let users send each other a single word, "Yo," and nothing else, which made it an instant novelty hit (reaching #4 on the iOS App Store) and drew over $2.5M in funding on the strength of that virality. But a one-word app had no real retention mechanic or monetization path once the novelty wore off, and founder Or Arbel moved on to other projects, leaving the company to fold while the app limped along unmaintained, later kept alive only through Patreon-funded volunteer support.
timingNote: A pure hype-cycle timing story — Yo rode a wave of "minimalist app" virality in 2014 that had nowhere to go once the joke stopped being novel; there was never a durable use case underneath the buzz.

name: Xmarks
tagline: A bookmark-sync tool that got acquired twice and outlived both parents' patience
proximateCause: LastPass, by then owned by LogMeIn, shut down the Xmarks bookmark-sync service for good on May 1, 2018.
rootCause: Xmarks (originally Foxmarks) struggled to turn its free bookmark-sync tool into a sustainable business, and after a failed 2010 push toward a $10-20/year premium model, it was acquired by LastPass in December 2010. When LogMeIn acquired LastPass in 2015, Xmarks became a legacy feature nobody was investing in, and as browsers built native bookmark sync directly into Chrome, Firefox, and Safari, the standalone product lost its reason to exist and was retired.
timingNote: A genuine timing failure — Xmarks solved a real problem in 2006-2010, but browser makers eventually built the same sync capability natively, making a third-party tool redundant by the late 2010s.

name: One Kings Lane
tagline: A luxury home-decor flash-sale site that survived three owners before bankruptcy caught up with it
proximateCause: One Kings Lane filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on April 23, 2023, as part of a joint filing with its then-parent, Bed Bath & Beyond.
rootCause: One Kings Lane raised over $200M and hit a $912M valuation by 2014 on the strength of flash-sale luxury home decor, but the flash-sale model's marketing costs and inventory risk made it unprofitable, and it was sold to Bed Bath & Beyond in 2016 for roughly $12M — a steep fall from its peak valuation. It moved to CSC Generation in 2020, but when Bed Bath & Beyond itself collapsed into bankruptcy in 2023, One Kings Lane was pulled down as a listed affiliate in the same filing.
timingNote: Not primarily a timing failure — home e-commerce and decor were durable categories — but a business-model failure: flash-sale economics never generated the margins needed to justify its early valuation, which compounded through two ownership changes into eventual bankruptcy.

name: VisiCalc
tagline: The first spreadsheet, made obsolete by the software category it invented
proximateCause: Lotus Development acquired Software Arts in 1985 and ended VisiCalc sales for good, closing out a product its own rival had already displaced commercially two years earlier.
rootCause: VisiCalc, built by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston, was the "killer app" that sold Apple II computers, with more than a quarter of 1979 Apple II buyers reportedly purchasing the machine specifically to run it. But when Lotus 1-2-3 launched in 1983 — built by a former VisiCorp employee to fully exploit the IBM PC's superior memory and display — VisiCalc's 8-bit-era architecture couldn't keep up, and its monthly sales collapsed from over 39,000 copies in January 1983 to just 5,700 by December of that year.
timingNote: A classic technology-shift timing failure — VisiCalc dominated the 8-bit Apple II era but was architecturally unable to take advantage of the 16-bit IBM PC wave that Lotus 1-2-3 rode to dominance.
